title: Anger Early Warning Map
summary: Traces the physical and cognitive build-up before an anger episode.
goal: Widen the gap between trigger and reaction.
body_md: Work backwards from a recent episode: what was the last moment a different choice was still available? That point, not the peak, is where the intervention goes.

fields.label: A recent episode — what happened
Body signs, earliest first
Thoughts that showed up
The last point you could still have stepped away
What you will do at that point next time
Who can flag it if you miss it

title: Boundary Script Builder
summary: Drafts and rehearses a specific boundary, sentence by sentence.
goal: Move boundary-setting from principle to a line the client can actually say.
body_md: Insist on one sentence with no justification attached. Clients tend to pad, and the padding is where the boundary leaks. Role-play the pushback in session — the second ask is the one people fold on.

fields.label: The situation
What I have been doing instead
My one-sentence boundary
What I expect them to say back
My reply to that
What I am afraid will happen
What is most likely to actually happen

title: Crisis Plan
summary: A written plan agreed in advance for a client's worst hours.
goal: Have a plan in place before it is needed, in the client's own words.
body_md: Complete it collaboratively and in session; a crisis plan sent home as homework rarely comes back. Keep the steps concrete enough to follow when distressed, and make sure means-restriction is discussed explicitly where it is relevant. Give the client a copy in the format they will actually have to hand.

fields.label: Signs I am heading for a crisis
Things that have helped me before
People I can contact, with numbers
Professionals, with numbers
How I will make my environment safer
Crisis line: 988 (call or text)
What I want others to do if I cannot ask

title: Grief Waves Record
summary: Tracks the shape of grief rather than measuring progress against it.
goal: Normalize the non-linearity of grief and identify triggers.
body_md: Explicitly frame this as noticing, not improving. Clients often arrive believing grief should decline steadily and read every wave as going backwards. Pay attention to anniversaries and sensory triggers.

fields.label: Date
What set it off, if anything
What the wave felt like in your body
How long it lasted
What helped, even slightly
What you would want on the next one

title: Self-Compassion Letter
summary: A letter to oneself in the voice used for a struggling friend.
goal: Loosen harsh self-criticism by borrowing a kinder perspective.
body_md: Have the client picture a specific friend first and write a line to them, then redirect the same words inward. Clients high in self-criticism often find this acutely uncomfortable — normalize that, and keep the first attempt short.

fields.label: What you are being hard on yourself about
What you would say to a friend in exactly this position
Now write it to yourself, by name
What was hard about writing that?

title: Sleep Diary and Hygiene Review
summary: Two weeks of sleep timings alongside the habits around them.
goal: Gather the data that CBT-I depends on.
body_md: Have the client fill it in on waking, from estimate rather than by clock-watching — checking the time in the night is itself a maintaining factor. Sleep efficiency below about 85% is where restriction usually starts earning its place.

fields.label: Date
Time to bed
Estimated time asleep
Times woken, and for how long
Time finally awake
Time out of bed
Caffeine, alcohol, screens after 8pm
Rested on waking? (0-10)

title: Social Support Map
summary: Maps the client's actual network by closeness and by what each person offers.
goal: Make isolation concrete, and find the nearest available connection.
body_md: Ask what each person is actually good for — practical help, listening, distraction, honesty — rather than ranking them. Clients often discover they have been taking every kind of need to one person.

fields.label: Name or initials
How close (inner circle / middle / outer)
What they are good for
Last contact
One person to reach out to this week

title: Values Compass
summary: Sorts life domains by importance against current attention.
goal: Find where a client's time and their values have come apart.
body_md: Rate importance and current attention separately, then look only at the gaps. The largest gap is usually the most useful place to work, and is often not the domain the client came in talking about.

fields.label: Domain (family, work, health, friendship, growth, community, play, spirituality)
How important is this to you? (0-10)
How much attention has it had lately? (0-10)
The gap
One small step that would close it this week

title: Activity and Mood Log
summary: An hour-by-hour record of what was done and how it felt.
goal: Establish a baseline and reveal the mood-behavior link before intervening.
body_md: Run this before behavioral activation, not instead of it. A week of data usually dismantles 'I do nothing and it's always terrible' more effectively than any amount of discussion.

fields.label: Day
Morning — what you did / mood (0-10)
Afternoon — what you did / mood (0-10)
Evening — what you did / mood (0-10)
Best moment of the day
Hardest moment

title: Behavioral Activation Weekly Planner
summary: Schedules activity by pleasure and mastery rather than by motivation.
goal: Break the withdrawal-low mood cycle in depression by acting before feeling.
duration: 20 minutes to plan, one week to run
body_md: The central message is that action precedes motivation, not the other way round. Start absurdly small — smaller than the client thinks is worth doing. Have them rate pleasure and mastery 0-10 immediately after each activity, not at the end of the week, or the depression will rewrite the record.

fields.label: Activity
Day and time planned
Predicted pleasure (0-10)
Predicted mastery (0-10)
Did it? (yes/no)
Actual pleasure (0-10)
Actual mastery (0-10)
What got in the way?

title: Behavioral Experiment Record
summary: Designs a real-world test of a specific prediction, then records what happened.
goal: Shift belief through lived disconfirmation rather than argument.
duration: One session to design, one week to run
body_md: The prediction must be specific and falsifiable before the experiment is worth running. 'It will go badly' is not testable; 'I will stammer and at least two people will look away' is. Write the prediction down before the experiment — memory is generous to the old belief afterwards.

fields.label: Belief being tested, and how strongly you hold it (0-100%)
The experiment — what exactly will you do?
Prediction — what specifically do you expect to happen?
What actually happened
What this says about the original belief
Re-rate the belief (0-100%)

title: Cognitive Distortions Field Guide
summary: The common thinking traps, each with a worked example and a reframe.
goal: Give clients shared language for spotting the shape of their own thinking.
body_md: Use as psychoeducation, then as a lookup while completing thought records. Ask the client which two or three are their signature traps rather than working through all of them — recognition matters more than coverage.

fields.label: Which traps do you notice most in yourself?
Write a recent thought and name the trap in it
Now rewrite that thought without the trap

title: Downward Arrow
summary: Follows a surface thought down to the core belief underneath it.
goal: Surface the belief driving a cluster of situations, not just this one.
body_md: Ask 'and if that were true, what would that mean about you?' repeatedly. Stop when the client reaches something absolute and self-referential ('I'm unlovable'). Go gently — this drops quickly into painful material, and needs enough session time left to come back up.

fields.label: Starting thought
If that were true, what would it mean?
...and what would that mean?
...and what would that mean?
The core belief underneath
Where do you think you first learned this?

title: Exposure Hierarchy
summary: Ranks feared situations by distress so exposure can proceed in steps.
goal: Structure graded exposure for phobia, social anxiety, panic or OCD.
body_md: Build ten to fifteen steps with SUDS ratings spread evenly from about 20 to 100. Steps clustered at the top mean the ladder needs more rungs at the bottom. Stay with each step until distress drops by roughly half, and repeat before moving up. Note any safety behaviors explicitly — exposure with them intact teaches the wrong lesson.

fields.label: Feared situation
Safety behaviors to drop for this step
Date attempted
Peak SUDS
SUDS at the end
What you learned

title: Panic Cycle Formulation
summary: Maps trigger, sensation, catastrophic interpretation and safety behavior as a loop.
goal: Show a client how the panic response feeds itself.
body_md: Draw it with the client rather than handing it over completed. The moment worth reaching is when they see the interpretation, not the sensation, is the hinge. Then identify which safety behaviors maintain the loop.

fields.label: Trigger
First body sensation you notice
What you take that to mean
What the fear does to the sensation
What you do to feel safer
How that keeps the cycle going

title: Relapse Prevention Plan
summary: Names early warning signs and the response to each, agreed while the client is well.
goal: Protect gains at the end of a piece of work.
body_md: Best written in the last two or three sessions. Distinguish a lapse from a relapse explicitly — clients who expect a straight line read the first bad week as total failure. Have them give a copy to someone who will notice.

fields.label: What I have learned that I want to keep
My early warning signs, in the order they usually appear
What has actually helped, ranked
What I will do in the first 48 hours of a wobble
Who I will tell, and what I want them to do
When I would contact a professional again

title: Seven-Column Thought Record
summary: The full Beckian thought record, from situation through to a re-rated emotion.
goal: Teach clients to catch, test and revise automatic thoughts in the moment.
body_md: Work the first two or three through in session before sending it home. Clients commonly jump straight to the balanced thought — slow them down at the evidence columns, which is where the therapeutic work actually happens. If a client writes 'I felt like a failure', separate the feeling (shame, 80%) from the thought ('I am a failure') before continuing.

fields.label: Situation — where were you, who was there, what happened?
Automatic thought — what went through your mind? Rate how much you believed it (0-100%)
Emotion — name it, and rate its intensity (0-100%)
Evidence that supports the thought
Evidence that does not support the thought
Balanced thought — what fits all the evidence?
Re-rate: belief in the original thought, and the emotion (0-100%)

title: Worry Tree
summary: Sorts worries into actionable and hypothetical, and routes each accordingly.
goal: Cut the time spent on worry that has no action attached to it.
body_md: The decision point is simply: can I do something about this today? If yes, make a plan and schedule it. If no, the work is refocusing attention rather than solving. Clients with GAD often insist every worry is actionable — expect to work on that.

fields.label: The worry
Is there anything you can do about it? (yes/no)
If yes: what, and when?
If no: what will you turn your attention to instead?
How strong was the worry before, and after? (0-10)

title: Committed Action Ladder
summary: Turns a value into graded, scheduled actions from easiest upward.
goal: Move from clarified values to behavior that actually happens.
body_md: The bottom rung should be something the client is 90% confident they will do. Track willingness rather than outcome — this is about showing up, not succeeding.

fields.label: The value this serves
Rung 1 (easiest)
Rung 2
Rung 3
Rung 4
Rung 5 (hardest)
Which rung this week, and when?
What showed up, and did you do it anyway?

title: Dropping the Rope
summary: A tug-of-war metaphor for ceasing the struggle with an internal monster.
goal: Illustrate that stopping the fight is available even when winning is not.
body_md: Physically act it out with a scarf or rope if the client is willing — the embodied version lands far harder than describing it. Ask what their hands are free to do once they let go.

fields.label: What is at the other end of your rope?
How long have you been pulling?
What would dropping it feel like?
What would your hands be free for?

title: Leaves on a Stream
summary: A guided defusion exercise placing each thought on a passing leaf.
goal: Practice watching thoughts rather than being carried by them.
body_md: Read it slowly, with real pauses. When the client says they got caught up and stopped, that is the exercise working, not failing — noticing the hook is the skill. Expect to normalize that several times.

fields.label: What showed up while you did this?
Where did you get hooked?
What was it like to watch instead of argue?

title: Life Compass Review
summary: A quarterly check of direction across all value domains at once.
goal: Give longer work a repeatable review point.
body_md: Useful every eight to twelve weeks. Compare against the last copy — clients notice drift they cannot see week to week.

fields.label: Domain
What matters to me here, in a sentence
How I have actually been showing up (0-10)
What gets in the way
One committed action for the next month

title: Observing Self Exercise
summary: Distinguishes the thinking self from the self that notices thinking.
goal: Build a stable vantage point that is not threatened by content.
body_md: Anchor it in continuity: the client noticing now is the same one who noticed at ten years old, though nearly everything else has changed. Go carefully with dissociative presentations — keep it brief and grounded.

fields.label: What did you notice noticing?
Has that noticing part ever been damaged by what it noticed?
What does that suggest about the thoughts you fear most?

title: The Passengers on the Bus
summary: A metaphor for driving toward values while difficult thoughts ride along.
goal: Separate the presence of difficult content from control over direction.
body_md: Draw the bus. Have the client name their loudest passengers in their own words, including the exact phrasing. The move is not throwing passengers off — it is keeping hands on the wheel while they shout.

fields.label: Where is your bus headed? (what matters to you)
Who are the loudest passengers, and what do they say?
What have you done to try to get them off?
What did that cost you?
What would driving on, with them aboard, look like today?

title: Values Card Sort
summary: Sorts values into most, somewhat and least important, then to a top five.
goal: Get to chosen values rather than inherited ones.
body_md: The forced narrowing to five is the whole point — clients resist it, and the resistance is worth exploring. Watch for values that are really other people's, or that are goals in disguise ('get promoted' is a goal; 'contribution' is a value).

fields.label: My top five values
For each: what would living it look like this week?
Which one have I been neglecting most?
What gets in the way?

title: Willingness and Struggle Diary
summary: Contrasts what the struggle with a feeling costs against willingness to have it.
goal: Make experiential avoidance and its price visible.
body_md: Focus on the cost column. Clients readily see that avoidance works short-term; the shift comes from tallying what it takes over a week.

fields.label: The feeling I did not want
What I did to avoid or control it
Did it work, short term?
What it cost me
What willingness could have looked like instead

title: Chain Analysis
summary: Reconstructs a problem behavior link by link, from vulnerability to consequence.
goal: Find the specific points where a different link was possible.
body_md: Slow and detailed is the point — aim for minute-by-minute in the run-up. Clients often want to skip to the behavior; the vulnerability factors earlier in the day are usually where the leverage is. Finish with repair as well as prevention.

fields.label: Vulnerability factors earlier that day
The prompting event
Links — thoughts, feelings, sensations, actions, in order
The problem behavior
Short-term consequences
Longer-term consequences
Where could a different link have gone in?
What repair is needed?

title: DEAR MAN Script Builder
summary: Builds an interpersonal-effectiveness request line by line.
goal: Ask for something clearly while keeping the relationship and self-respect intact.
body_md: Have the client write each letter out in full and then say it aloud. Most people collapse Describe and Express into judgment — hold the line on describing facts only. Rehearse the refusal too.

fields.label: Describe — the facts, no interpretation
Express — how you feel about it, using 'I'
Assert — what you are actually asking for
Reinforce — what is in it for them
Mindful — the one line you return to if they deflect
Appear confident — posture, voice, eye contact
Negotiate — what you can give ground on

title: Distress Tolerance ACCEPTS
summary: Seven ways to get through a bad hour without making it worse.
goal: Give clients options for surviving a crisis without acting on the urge.
body_md: Have the client pre-fill their own examples in session; a generic list will not be reached for at 2am. Be clear these are for getting through, not for solving.

fields.label: Activities — mine are
Contributing — mine are
Comparisons — mine are
Emotions (opposite) — mine are
Pushing away — how I do it
Thoughts — mine are
Sensations — mine are

title: Emotion Regulation Diary Card
summary: Daily ratings of emotions, urges and skills used.
goal: Provide the week's data for a skills review or chain analysis.
body_md: Review it at the start of every session without exception — a card that is never looked at stops being filled in. Rate urges and actions separately.

fields.label: Date
Emotions and intensity (0-5)
Urges — self-harm, substances, other (0-5)
Acted on any urge? (yes/no)
Skills used today
How helpful were they? (0-5)

title: Opposite Action Planner
summary: Identifies the action urge in an emotion and plans the opposite, fully committed.
goal: Change an emotion that does not fit the facts by acting against its urge.
body_md: First check whether the emotion fits the facts — opposite action is for when it does not, or when acting on it makes things worse. Half-hearted opposite action does not work; the 'all the way' part is not optional, and worth naming.

fields.label: The emotion, and how strong (0-100)
Does it fit the facts?
The urge that comes with it
The opposite action, in full
How to do it all the way
How strong is the emotion afterwards? (0-100)

title: Radical Acceptance Steps
summary: Works through accepting a reality that cannot currently be changed.
goal: Reduce the added suffering that fighting an unchangeable fact produces.
body_md: Distinguish acceptance from approval early and often — clients hear 'accept it' as 'it was fine'. Acceptance is repeated rather than achieved; expect to come back to it.

fields.label: The reality I am fighting
How I know it is what it is
What the fighting has cost me
What acceptance would NOT mean
How my life could go on from here
What I will do when the fighting starts again

title: TIPP Crisis Skills Card
summary: Temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing and paired relaxation, on one card.
goal: Bring extreme arousal down fast enough for other skills to be usable.
body_md: This is a physiological intervention, not a coping conversation — teach it when the client is calm and rehearse it. Ask about heart conditions and any history of restrictive eating before recommending cold water or intense exercise.

fields.label: Temperature — cold water on the face, holding your breath, 30 seconds
Intense exercise — 10 minutes, hard enough to be breathless
Paced breathing — out longer than in, 5 minutes
Paired muscle relaxation — tense on the in-breath, release on the out
Which of these will you actually use? Where will this card live?

title: Wise Mind Practice
summary: Locates the overlap between emotion mind and reasonable mind.
goal: Help clients find a decision-making state that is neither purely feeling nor purely logic.
body_md: Draw the two overlapping circles. Ask for a recent decision made from each state and how it turned out. Wise mind is recognized by a settled quality rather than certainty.

fields.label: A recent emotion-mind decision, and what happened
A recent reasonable-mind decision, and what happened
A decision you face now
What does wise mind say about it?
How do you know it is wise mind and not something else?

title: Conflict Pattern Map
summary: Maps the couple's recurring cycle: each partner's move, meaning and protection.
goal: Get the couple looking at the pattern together rather than at each other.
body_md: Externalize the cycle and give it a name they choose. The reframe worth reaching is that both are protecting themselves, and the protection is what triggers the other.

fields.label: What usually starts it
What A does
What B takes that to mean
What B does
What A takes that to mean
What each of you is protecting
What we will call this cycle
The earliest point either of us could name it

title: Love Maps Questionnaire
summary: Structured questions about each other's inner world, present and future.
goal: Rebuild knowledge of a partner that has drifted.
body_md: Works well as homework then reviewed in session. Watch for the confident wrong answers — assuming you know is more corrosive than not knowing.

fields.label: What is currently stressing them most?
Who are their closest people right now?
What are they most looking forward to?
What are they quietly worried about?
What do they need more of from you?
What would a good year look like to them?

title: Needs and Bids Log
summary: Records bids for connection and how they were answered over a week.
goal: Make turning-toward and turning-away visible and countable.
body_md: Most bids are tiny and easily missed — a comment about the weather is often a bid. Counting them usually surprises both partners.

fields.label: Day
A bid I made
How it was answered (toward / away / against)
A bid I noticed from them
How I answered it
What I would do differently

title: Repair Attempt Checklist
summary: A shared list of phrases each partner can use, and agrees to accept, mid-conflict.
goal: Give couples a way to de-escalate before flooding takes over.
body_md: The agreement to *receive* a repair matters more than the phrasing. Have them choose the exact words together — borrowed scripts get ignored. Pair with a break agreement: who calls it, how long, and who restarts.

fields.label: Phrases I can say when it is getting heated
Phrases I will accept from you
Our word or signal for needing a break
How long our breaks last
Who restarts the conversation, and when

title: Shared Meaning and Rituals
summary: Identifies rituals of connection worth protecting or creating.
goal: Give a relationship structure that survives busy periods.
body_md: Focus on small and repeatable over grand gestures — the coffee before anyone else wakes beats the annual holiday. Get specific about when, or it will not happen.

fields.label: Rituals we already have, however small
Which ones have slipped
One we want to protect, and how
One new one we want to try, starting when
What we want this relationship to stand for

title: Softened Start-Up Rewrite
summary: Rewrites a harsh opening into a complaint about behavior rather than character.
goal: Change how conversations begin, which largely determines how they end.
body_md: Have each partner bring a real recent opener. Rewrite it together in session: 'I feel ___ about ___ and I need ___.' Practice saying it aloud to each other — reading it off the page does not transfer.

fields.label: The harsh version you actually used
What you were feeling underneath it
What you actually needed
Your softened version: I feel ___ about ___, I need ___
How it landed when you said it

title: Weekly Appreciation Exchange
summary: A standing five minutes of specific, behavioral appreciation.
goal: Rebuild the positive-to-negative ratio that predicts stability.
body_md: Specificity is everything — 'you're a good partner' does nothing; 'you took the bins out on Tuesday when I was flattened' does. Same time each week, and no requests allowed inside the exercise.

fields.label: Something specific you did this week that I appreciated
What it meant to me
Something I noticed you finding hard
One thing I am looking forward to with you

title: Body Clues Detective
summary: The child marks on an outline where feelings show up in their body.
goal: Build interoceptive awareness as an early warning system.
body_md: Use a different color per feeling. Children often locate anxiety in the stomach and anger in the hands and face — link those clues to the thermometer levels so the child can catch a feeling early.

fields.label: Where do you feel worried?
Where do you feel angry?
Where do you feel sad?
Where do you feel happy?
Which clue shows up first?
What do you do when you notice it?

title: Brave Ladder
summary: A child-friendly exposure hierarchy drawn as a ladder with rewards.
goal: Structure graded exposure for childhood anxiety with the child on board.
body_md: Draw an actual ladder. The child chooses the rewards and they must be immediate. Involve the parent in what accommodation they will stop providing — that is often the harder half of the work.

fields.label: My brave goal at the top
Step 1 (easiest) — my reward
Step 2 — my reward
Step 3 — my reward
Step 4 — my reward
Step 5 — my reward
Who is my brave helper?
What grown-ups will stop doing for me

title: Calm-Down Kit Planner
summary: Plans a physical box of sensory items the child chooses.
goal: Make self-soothing concrete and available at home and school.
body_md: The child picks the items or the box will not get used. Cover all five senses if you can. Rehearse using it when calm — nobody learns a new skill mid-meltdown.

fields.label: Something to touch
Something to look at
Something to listen to
Something to smell
Something to taste or chew
Where my box lives at home
Where my box lives at school
Who reminds me to use it

title: Feelings Thermometer
summary: A drawable scale from calm to biggest feeling, with coping steps at each level.
goal: Give a child language and a scale for intensity before it peaks.
body_md: Have the child color it and name each level themselves — their words, not clinical ones ('volcano' beats 'severe distress'). Send a copy home and one to school so the same language is used everywhere.

fields.label: Level 1 — what it looks like, what helps
Level 2 — what it looks like, what helps
Level 3 — what it looks like, what helps
Level 4 — what it looks like, what helps
Level 5 — what it looks like, who helps me
How grown-ups can tell which level I am at

title: Parent Coaching Sheet: Labeled Praise
summary: A one-page parent handout on descriptive praise with practice tracking.
goal: Increase wanted behavior by changing what parents notice out loud.
duration: 15 minutes to teach, one week to practice
body_md: Give parents a specific target — five labeled praises a day, tracked. 'Good boy' is not labeled praise; 'you put your shoes away without being asked' is. Expect parents to find this harder and more artificial than they anticipate at first.

fields.label: Behavior I want more of
My labeled praise for it, word for word
Day 1-7: how many times I said it
What I noticed in my child
What got in the way

title: Superhero Strengths Card
summary: The child designs a superhero version of themselves built from real strengths.
goal: Build self-concept in children with low self-worth.
body_md: Every power has to trace back to something they actually do. Gather evidence from parents and teachers beforehand if the child struggles to generate any.

fields.label: My superhero name
My powers — and what I really do that shows each one
My weakness (everyone has one)
Who is on my team?
A time I used a power for real

title: Three Good Things Jar
summary: A daily written note of something good, collected in a jar.
goal: Build attentional bias toward the positive, and a resource for low days.
body_md: The jar being visible matters. On hard days the child reads old notes rather than adding new ones. Get the family doing it too, not just the child.

fields.label: Something good that happened today
Something I did well
Someone who was kind to me
Read three old notes on a hard day

title: Worry Monster Externalizing Craft
summary: The child draws and names their worry as a character, then talks back to it.
goal: Separate the child from the worry so it can be addressed rather than embodied.
body_md: Let the child name it. Once the worry is a character with a voice, ask what it says, then what the child would say back. Some children want to keep the drawing; some want to post it in a box. Both are fine.

fields.label: Draw your worry — what does it look like?
What is its name?
What does it say to you?
When does it show up most?
What do you want to say back to it?
Who helps you when it is loud?

title: Emotion Jenga
summary: Jenga blocks marked with prompts, answered before each pull.
goal: Lower the pressure of disclosure by attaching it to a game.
body_md: Mix easy prompts with harder ones so the tower does not become an interrogation. The physical tension of the game gives children somewhere to put their nerves while talking. Let them pass twice per game.

fields.label: Prompts on our blocks
Which prompt was hardest
Something I learned about someone else
Something I said out loud for the first time

title: Feelings Charades
summary: Acting and guessing emotions without words.
goal: Build emotion recognition and expression in a low-pressure way.
body_md: Start with the big four, then add subtler ones (disappointed, embarrassed, relieved). Ask what gave it away — that question is where the learning is. Works well in family sessions with parents taking turns too.

fields.label: Emotions to use
Who guessed what
Which were hardest to show
Which were hardest to read
What clues we used

title: Reframe Tennis
summary: Players volley a negative thought back and forth as reframes.
goal: Practice cognitive flexibility at speed, competitively.
body_md: The pace is the point — it stops the over-thinking that stalls thought records. Rule out toxic positivity explicitly: a reframe must be believable, not cheerful. First person who cannot volley concedes the point.

fields.label: Starting thought
Reframes we generated
Which reframe was actually believable
Which ones were just positive thinking

title: The Coping Skills Deck
summary: A card game where players draw a scenario and a skill, and argue for the fit.
goal: Rehearse skill selection before it is needed under pressure.
body_md: Deliberate mismatches are the best part — defending why a bad pairing might work generates more discussion than the obvious fits. Have the group build the deck themselves over a few sessions.

fields.label: Scenario cards we made
Skill cards we made
Best pairing this session, and why
A mismatch that turned out to make sense

title: The Values Auction
summary: Players bid a fixed budget on values in an open auction.
goal: Force prioritization and surface what a client will actually spend on.
body_md: Give everyone the same budget. What people overspend on, and what they let go without a fight, is the material — debrief on that rather than on who won.

fields.label: What I bid on, and how much
What I won
What I let go without bidding
What surprised me about my own bidding
What I would do differently

title: Two Truths and a Coping Lie
summary: A group icebreaker adapted to coping strategies.
goal: Open a group and surface strategies that only look helpful.
body_md: Each person gives two things that genuinely help them and one that seems helpful but costs them. The group guesses. It gets at avoidance without anyone being singled out.

fields.label: My two real coping strategies
My one that only looks like coping
What the group guessed
What I noticed in other people's answers

title: Burnout Energy Audit
summary: A week of tasks sorted by what they cost and what they give back.
goal: Separate exhaustion that rest will fix from exhaustion that only a change will fix.
body_md: Ask for a real week, not a typical one. The useful column is the drain-to-return ratio, not the hours; clients are often surprised that the heaviest cost is a small task they resent. Use the last two prompts to open a conversation about what is negotiable, and be honest when nothing on the list is.

fields.label: The tasks and roles that filled my week
For each: how much it drained me (0-10)
For each: how much it gave back (0-10)
The three worst ratios
Which of those I could drop, shrink or hand off
Which I cannot change, and what I would need to carry them
One recovery activity I will protect this week

title: Perfectionism Cost-Benefit Sheet
summary: Weighs what a client's standards buy them against what the standards charge.
goal: Loosen the belief that high standards are the only thing standing between the client and failure.
body_md: Take the benefits seriously and write them down first; a client who feels their standards are being attacked will defend them. The costs usually emerge in the prompts about time, relationships and what never gets started. Close by drafting one standard at the level of good enough and agreeing to test it.

fields.label: A standard I hold myself to
What it has genuinely got me
What it costs me in time
What it costs the people around me
Things I have not started because I could not do them perfectly
What good enough would look like for this standard
One place I will try good enough this week

title: Procrastination Loop Map
summary: Traces the feeling, the escape and the relief that keep a task undone.
goal: Show the client that avoidance is a working loop, not a character flaw, and find its weakest link.
body_md: Draw it as a circle in session. The relief step is the engine and most clients have never named it. Aim the intervention at the first two minutes of the task, not the whole task, and treat the plan as an experiment to report back on rather than a promise.

fields.label: The task I keep putting off
What I feel when I think about starting
What I do instead
How I feel right after escaping
How I feel later that day
The smallest first step that would take under two minutes
When and where I will take it

title: Decision Balance Sheet
summary: Four boxes for the gains and losses of changing and of staying the same.
goal: Bring ambivalence into the open so it can be worked with instead of argued against.
body_md: Fill the staying-the-same boxes as fully as the change boxes; that is what makes this different from a pep talk. Do not resolve the ambivalence for the client. Ask which box they had the most to say about, and let that be the material for the next session.

fields.label: The change I am considering
Good things about staying as I am
Not-so-good things about staying as I am
Good things about making the change
Not-so-good things about making the change
On a scale of 0-10, how important is this change to me, and why not lower
What would move me one point up

title: Session Bridge Sheet
summary: A short review completed before each session, linking last week to this one.
goal: Make each session start from what actually happened rather than from what is loudest today.
body_md: Send it two days before the session or have the client complete it in the waiting room. The value is in the third and fourth prompts: what got tried and what got in the way. Read it aloud together at the start and set the agenda from it.

fields.label: What I took away from last session
What I tried between sessions
What got in the way, if anything
What has been on my mind this week
What I want to make sure we cover today
How I have been, 0-10

title: Safety Behaviors Inventory
summary: Lists the small things a client does to feel safer, and what each one prevents them learning.
goal: Find the behaviors that keep a fear alive so they can be dropped inside exposure work.
body_md: Clients rarely think of these as behaviors; ask what they would never do without, what they carry, who they bring, and what they check. The prediction column is where the learning happens: dropping a safety behavior only teaches something if the feared outcome was named first.

fields.label: The situation I fear
Things I do or carry to get through it
What each one is meant to stop happening
What I have therefore never found out
The one I will drop first
What I predict will happen without it (0-100% sure)
What actually happened

title: Positive Data Log
summary: A running record of evidence that supports a new, kinder core belief.
goal: Build a new belief by collecting what the old belief filters out.
duration: Five minutes daily for several weeks
body_md: Word the new belief in the client's own language before starting and keep it modest. Clients discount small evidence, so teach them to log the small stuff deliberately. Review the log in session and rate belief in both the old and the new statement each time.

fields.label: The old belief and how much I believe it (0-100%)
The new belief I am testing and how much I believe it (0-100%)
Date
Something that happened that fits the new belief, however small
What I would normally have done with this evidence
Belief in the new statement now (0-100%)

title: Responsibility Pie Chart
summary: Divides a feared or regretted outcome among every factor that contributed to it.
goal: Shrink inflated responsibility by putting it on the same page as everyone and everything else involved.
body_md: List every contributing factor before assigning any percentages, and put the client's own slice in last; done in the other order the client claims most of the pie. Works for guilt, for OCD responsibility beliefs and for a parent blaming themselves for a child's difficulty. Draw the actual circle.

fields.label: What happened, or what I fear will happen
Everyone and everything that contributed
How much of the outcome belongs to each (%)
My slice, added last
How much I believed it was my fault before this (0-100%)
How much now

title: Worry Postponement Schedule
summary: A fixed daily worry period, with a log for the worries that arrive outside it.
goal: Break the habit of worrying whenever worry shows up, and show the client that postponed worries lose their urgency.
body_md: Agree on a worry period of about twenty minutes at the same time each day, not near bedtime. Everything outside it gets written down and postponed, not suppressed. Most clients report that at least half of the postponed worries have gone stale by the time the period arrives, which is the point to draw out in session.

fields.label: My daily worry period: when and where
Worries that showed up outside it (write and postpone)
At the worry period: which still mattered
Which had gone stale
What I did during the worry period with the ones that mattered
How hard was postponing today (0-10)

title: Reassurance Seeking Log
summary: Tracks every request for reassurance, what it relieved and how long that lasted.
goal: Make the short half-life of reassurance visible, and plan how to tolerate the doubt instead.
body_md: Include the quiet forms: checking online, rereading a message, asking the same question a different way. The duration column does the work. Involve partners or parents in what they will say instead of answering, and agree the wording in session so it does not sound like a rejection.

fields.label: Date and time
What I was worried about
Who or what I asked, and how
Relief straight after (0-10)
How long the relief lasted
What I could have done with the doubt instead
What the people around me will say next time instead of reassuring

title: Thank Your Mind Practice
summary: A defusion habit of noticing a sticky thought and thanking the mind for it.
goal: Change the client's relationship with a thought without arguing with its content.
duration: 5 minutes to teach, then in the moment
body_md: Model it with one of your own thoughts first so it does not sound like sarcasm. The tone is warm, as toward an over-helpful friend. Follow with the question of what the mind is trying to protect; clients find it easier to unhook from a thought once they can see its job.

fields.label: The thought my mind keeps offering
What my mind might be trying to protect me from
The thank-you I will use (in my own words)
When I tried it this week
What changed, even slightly

title: Choice Point Map
summary: A one-page map of a difficult situation, the hooks it brings and the toward and away moves available.
goal: Give the client a single picture of the moment of choice they meet again and again.
body_md: Draw the fork in session. Be strict that away moves are defined by their function, not by what they look like; scrolling can be a toward move if it is a chosen rest. Fill the toward side with things the client has done before, not ideals, and ask which skill from the toolkit helps at the fork.

fields.label: The situation I keep meeting
The thoughts and feelings that show up (the hooks)
My usual away moves
What those away moves cost me
Toward moves I have made before in this situation
The values behind the toward moves
The skill I will use at the fork next time

title: Struggle Switch Dial
summary: Rates how hard the client is fighting a feeling, separately from how strong the feeling is.
goal: Show the client that the struggle, not the feeling, is what they can turn down.
body_md: Introduce the two dials with a recent example where a feeling was tolerable and one where it was not; the difference is usually the second dial. Practice turning the struggle dial down in session with a mild discomfort before asking the client to try it with anxiety.

fields.label: A feeling I have been fighting
How strong it has been (0-10)
How hard I have been fighting it (0-10)
What fighting it looks like for me
What happened to the feeling when I fought it
What I noticed when I let the fight dial drop, even by one

title: Values Bullseye
summary: A dartboard with four life areas, marked with how close the client is living to each value.
goal: Get a quick, visual reading of the gap between values and daily life in four domains.
body_md: Have the client write one sentence of value for each quadrant before placing any marks, or the marks become a mood rating. It repeats well every few sessions as a progress measure. Ask about the barriers only for the quadrant with the widest gap.

fields.label: Work and education: what matters to me here
Leisure: what matters to me here
Relationships: what matters to me here
Personal growth and health: what matters to me here
For each: how close to the center am I living (1 = far, 7 = bullseye)
What stands between me and the center in the widest gap
One move toward the center this week

title: I'm Having the Thought That
summary: A three-step language practice that puts distance between the client and a thought.
goal: Teach the client to hear a thought as a thought rather than as a fact.
body_md: Run all three steps out loud in session: the bare thought, then with I am having the thought that, then with I notice I am having the thought that. Ask what changed in the body at each step. Pick a thought with real charge but not the most painful one on the first pass.

fields.label: The thought, as it usually arrives
I'm having the thought that...
I notice I'm having the thought that...
What shifted between the first and last version
Where I will use this during the week

title: GIVE Skills Planner
summary: Prepares a conversation where the relationship matters more than the outcome.
goal: Help the client ask or refuse in a way the relationship survives.
body_md: Pair it with DEAR MAN: that script says what to say, this one says how. Gentle, Interested, Validate, Easy manner. Role-play the validation line; clients often write a validation that is actually a concession. The manner column is best rehearsed with a timer, since easy manner disappears under pressure.

fields.label: The conversation, and why the relationship matters here
Gentle: what I will not do (attacks, threats, judging, eye-rolling)
Interested: the question I will ask them, and how I will listen
Validate: what I can honestly acknowledge about their position
Easy manner: how I will keep it light
How it went, and what I would keep

title: FAST Self-Respect Check
summary: A review of a recent interaction against the four self-respect skills.
goal: Help the client hold their own values in an interaction instead of trading them for approval.
body_md: Fair, no Apologies, Stick to values, Truthful. The over-apologizing prompt is the one most clients recognize immediately. Use a real recent interaction and be specific about what the extra apology or the small lie bought. Plan the next interaction with the values line written in advance.

fields.label: A recent interaction where I lost some self-respect
Fair: was I fair to myself as well as to them
No apologies: what I apologized for that needed no apology
Stick to values: where I gave ground I did not want to give
Truthful: what I said that was not quite true, and why
What I will do differently next time

title: PLEASE Skills Tracker
summary: A daily check on the physical basics that make emotions harder or easier to regulate.
goal: Reduce emotional vulnerability by attending to illness, eating, substances, sleep and exercise.
duration: Two minutes daily for a week
body_md: Frame this as lowering the water line, not fixing the emotions. Look for the pattern across the week rather than any single day; the link between a bad night and the next afternoon's blow-up is usually the finding. Keep the exercise bar low, and never turn the eating prompt into a diet.

fields.label: Date
Physical illness: anything I am ignoring or not treating
Eating: did I eat regularly and enough today
Mood-altering substances: what I used, including caffeine and alcohol
Sleep: hours, and quality (0-10)
Exercise: any movement today
My emotional vulnerability today (0-10) and what I notice

title: Urge Pros and Cons Grid
summary: Four boxes weighing acting on a crisis urge against tolerating it, filled in ahead of time.
goal: Give the client a completed grid to read in the moment, when they cannot think one up.
body_md: Complete it in session while calm, and make the pros of acting on the urge honest; a grid that pretends there is no upside will be ignored at 2 a.m. Add the long-term column explicitly. Have the client photograph it and decide where it lives on their phone.

fields.label: The urge this grid is for
Pros of acting on the urge (be honest)
Cons of acting on the urge, short term and long term
Pros of tolerating the urge, short term and long term
Cons of tolerating the urge
What I will read first when the urge is at its strongest
Where this grid lives so I can find it

title: Check the Facts
summary: Tests whether an emotion fits the facts of the event, and whether its size fits.
goal: Decide whether an emotion should be acted on, problem-solved or changed with opposite action.
body_md: Keep the event description free of interpretation; that step alone often shifts the emotion. The threat prompt is where catastrophizing shows up, so ask for the probability out loud. If the emotion fits the facts, move to problem solving rather than opposite action, and say so plainly.

fields.label: The emotion, and its intensity (0-100)
The event that prompted it: only what a camera would have recorded
My interpretations and assumptions about the event
Other ways of seeing it
Am I assuming a threat? How likely is it, really (0-100%)
If the worst happened, how would I cope
Does the emotion fit the facts? Does its size? What I will do next

title: Four Horsemen Spotter
summary: Each partner identifies their own criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling, and the antidote for each.
goal: Give a couple a shared, low-blame vocabulary for what goes wrong in their arguments.
body_md: Each partner completes it about themselves only, never about the other; enforce that gently, since the temptation is strong. Contempt deserves the most time and the most care. Finish with each partner choosing one antidote to practice and telling the other what it will sound like.

fields.label: Criticism: how it sounds when I do it
Contempt: how it shows up in me (tone, face, jokes)
Defensiveness: my usual counterattack or excuse
Stonewalling: what shutting down looks like for me, and what I need to come back
The horseman I ride most
The antidote I will practice (gentle start-up, appreciation, taking responsibility, self-soothing)
What my partner will hear when I get it right

title: Stress-Reducing Conversation Guide
summary: A structured daily conversation about stress from outside the relationship.
goal: Teach a couple to support each other about outside stress without turning it into a fight about the relationship.
body_md: The rule is that the stress must come from outside the relationship. Teach the listener role in session: understanding before advice, taking the partner's side, no problem solving unless asked. Most couples need the listener prompts on paper for the first two weeks.

fields.label: Speaker: what is stressing me outside our relationship
Listener: what I heard, in my own words
Listener: what I said to take their side
Listener: did I offer advice? Was it asked for?
Speaker: what I needed from the conversation, and whether I got it
One thing we will change about how we did this

title: Dreams Within Conflict
summary: An interview for a gridlocked issue, uncovering the hope or history underneath each position.
goal: Turn a perpetual, stuck argument into a conversation about what each partner is protecting.
body_md: Only for gridlocked issues, not solvable ones. Each partner interviews the other for about ten minutes and may not persuade, correct or interrupt; you hold that boundary. The questions about childhood and about what the position means to them are the ones that open things up. Do not aim for a solution in this session.

fields.label: The issue we cannot get past
My position on it
What this position means to me, and where it comes from
What I am afraid would happen if I gave it up
The dream or value underneath my position
What I learned about my partner's dream
What parts of this I could be flexible on, and what I cannot

title: Aftermath of a Fight Debrief
summary: A five-step structured conversation for processing a fight after both partners are calm.
goal: Let a couple learn from a regrettable incident without reopening it.
body_md: Wait at least a day and check both partners are calm before starting. Each partner describes their own reality of the fight without interruption, and the other summarizes it back before adding their own. Triggers from past history are the richest step and the one to slow down on. End with one concrete change each.

fields.label: How I felt during the fight (name feelings, not their behavior)
My reality of what happened
My partner's reality, as I understood it
What this fight triggered from my past
My part in it, and what I take responsibility for
One thing I will do differently next time
One thing I need from my partner next time

title: Raw Spots and Reaching
summary: Each partner names their attachment raw spots and what a reach for the other would look like.
goal: Move a couple from protest and withdrawal toward direct, softer reaching.
body_md: Belongs in the middle of EFT work, after the cycle has been mapped. Slow down on the raw-spot prompts and stay with the softer emotion under the protest. The reaching prompt should be written in the second person and spoken to the partner in session, with you keeping the other partner receptive.

fields.label: The raw spot that gets touched most in our cycle
What I do when it gets touched (protest, pursue, withdraw, shut down)
The softer feeling underneath that move
What I fear my partner would think if they saw that feeling
What I actually need from my partner in that moment
How I would say it to them directly, in my own words
What I need to hear back

title: Worry Time Box
summary: A decorated box where a child posts written worries to be opened at a set time with a parent.
goal: Contain worry to one part of the day, with a parent as the reliable listener.
body_md: Let the child decorate the box; ownership matters. Agree the worry time with the parent and keep it short and not at bedtime. Coach the parent to open the box with curiosity and without fixing, and to notice with the child which worries have gone quiet by the time they are read.

fields.label: My worry box looks like
Our worry time is (when and with whom)
Worries I posted this week
Worries that did not seem as big when we opened the box
Worries that still needed help
What my grown-up said that helped

title: Anger Volcano Map
summary: A volcano drawing that shows a child's anger rising from rumbles to eruption.
goal: Help a child notice anger early and choose a cooling step before the top.
body_md: Draw a big volcano and let the child fill in the levels in their own words. The rumble level is what to spend time on; children usually only know the eruption. Practice one cooling step in session and make sure a parent or teacher knows the child's rumble signs.

fields.label: Things that make my lava start to bubble
Rumbles: how my body tells me it is starting
Getting hot: what I do and say when it grows
Eruption: what happens at the top
My cool-down move at rumble level
My cool-down move at getting hot
A grown-up who can spot my rumbles

title: Belly Breathing Buddy
summary: Slow breathing practice with a small stuffed toy riding on the child's stomach.
goal: Teach diaphragmatic breathing to a child through play rather than instruction.
body_md: Lying down, toy on the belly, the job is to rock the buddy to sleep slowly. Count the breaths out loud together at first, breathing out longer than in. Do it when the child is calm so it is available when they are not; a skill taught mid-meltdown does not stick.

fields.label: My breathing buddy's name
How my buddy moves when I breathe slowly
When I practiced this week
A time I used it when I felt wobbly
How my body felt after

title: Bedtime Routine Builder
summary: A picture-and-words plan for the last hour before sleep, built with the child.
goal: Give a child a predictable wind-down that a parent can hold consistently.
body_md: Build it with the child and the parent in the room. Keep it to five or six steps in the same order every night, with screens finished before it begins. The prompt about what happens when the child gets up again is the one parents most need agreed in advance, in a calm, boring script.

fields.label: Our bedtime is
Step 1 (screens are off)
Step 2
Step 3
Step 4
Step 5: lights out words we always say
What my grown-up will do if I get up again
How the first week went

title: Parent Coaching Sheet: Special Time
summary: Five minutes a day of child-led play where the parent follows, describes and praises.
goal: Strengthen the parent-child relationship so that limits later carry more weight.
duration: 15 minutes to teach, then five minutes daily
body_md: Teach the parent to describe what the child is doing, reflect what the child says and praise specifics, and to avoid questions, commands and criticism during the five minutes. Rehearse it in session with the parent playing while you describe. The log prompt about what was hardest to hold back is where coaching happens.

fields.label: When special time will happen each day
Toys or activities that work for following the child's lead
Date and what we played
Things I described and praised
What I found hardest to hold back (questions, commands, corrections)
How my child responded
What I noticed in the rest of the day

title: Feelings Bingo
summary: Bingo cards of feeling words, marked when a player shares a time they felt each one.
goal: Build emotion vocabulary and easy disclosure in a group or family.
body_md: Make the cards from a word bank the group builds first, so every card has feelings they actually know. A square is marked only after a short real example. Mix mild feelings with big ones and let players skip a square twice. Play a second round with body sensations instead of words if the group is ready.

fields.label: Feeling words we put on our cards
The squares I marked, with my examples
A feeling word that was new to me
A feeling I heard someone else describe that I have had too
A square I skipped, and why

title: Would You Rather: Coping Edition
summary: Pairs of coping choices, argued for and against by the group before anyone votes.
goal: Get a group talking about what helps and what backfires without anyone having to own a struggle.
body_md: Write the pairs so neither option is obviously right: call a friend or go for a run, cry it out or distract, tell someone or wait a day. Everyone argues both sides before voting. The debrief prompt about which choices depend on the situation is where the group's coping wisdom comes out.

fields.label: The pairs we used
My picks and my reasons
A pick where I was in the minority
Which choices depend on the situation
A coping option I had not considered before

title: Thought Detective
summary: Players investigate a suspect thought by gathering clues for and against it.
goal: Make evidence-checking feel like a case to solve rather than a form to fill in.
body_md: Give the child a notebook and a magnifying glass if you have one. The thought is the suspect, and the child collects clues that support it and clues that do not, then delivers a verdict. Play it first with a thought that is clearly untrue to teach the moves, then with one of their own.

fields.label: The suspect thought
Clues that say it is true
Clues that say it is not true
Clues I had to go and look for
The detective's verdict: true, not true, or only partly true
A fairer thought, based on all the clues

title: Compliment Toss
summary: A soft ball thrown around the circle; the thrower gives a specific compliment to the catcher.
goal: Practice giving and receiving specific praise in a group, with the awkwardness built in.
body_md: Compliments must be specific and about something the person did or said in the group, not their appearance. Model the first one. Receiving is half the game: the catcher says thank you and nothing else, and the leader stops any deflecting. Ask afterward which was harder, giving or getting.

fields.label: A compliment I gave
A compliment I got
What I wanted to say instead of thank you
Which was harder, giving or receiving
Something I noticed about someone that I did not get to say

title: Emotion Dice
summary: One die names a feeling and one names a prompt; players answer the combination they roll.
goal: Lower the stakes of talking about feelings by leaving the choice of feeling to chance.
body_md: Label one die with feelings and one with prompts such as a time I felt this, what my body does, what helps, who I would tell. Chance removes the sense of being singled out. Keep two passes per player, and take your own turns so the group sees an adult answer plainly.

fields.label: Feelings on our die
Prompts on our other die
The combinations I rolled and what I said
A combination someone else rolled that I could have answered too
The roll I passed on

title: Life Timeline Review
summary: A line across the page marked with the turning points of the client's life, high and low.
goal: Give the client and clinician a shared map of where the present difficulties sit in a longer story.
body_md: Draw one long line and let the client place events above it for good and below it for hard. Ask about the gaps as much as the marks; a quiet decade is often where something was being held. Keep the pace theirs and stop at any point that is too much for today; the timeline can be finished later.

fields.label: The events I would put above the line
The events I would put below the line
A stretch with nothing on it, and what was going on then
The turning point that matters most to what I am dealing with now
A strength I can see running through the line
What I want the next part of the line to look like

title: Adult Wind-Down Plan
summary: The last hour before bed planned step by step, with screens, worry and caffeine each given a cutoff.
goal: Give an adult a predictable path to sleep instead of a nightly negotiation with the phone.
body_md: Start from the wake time the client needs and work backward to fix the bedtime. The plan is only as good as the screen cutoff, so agree where the phone will physically be. Pair with the sleep diary when the client wants evidence; most see the change within two weeks if the plan is the same every night.

fields.label: The time I need to be asleep, working back from when I must be up
Caffeine cutoff
Screen cutoff, and where the phone goes
The three steps of my wind-down, in order
What I will do with worries that arrive in bed (write them down for tomorrow)
What I will do if I am still awake after twenty minutes
How the first week went

title: Money Stress Map
summary: Separates the parts of a money worry that are facts, decisions, feelings and fears.
goal: Bring some order to a stress that usually arrives as one undifferentiated dread.
body_md: You are not a financial adviser and the sheet does not give money advice; it sorts the worry so the client can act on the parts that are actionable and feel the parts that are feelings. Watch for shame, which stops people opening envelopes. The next-step prompt should be tiny: open one letter, make one call.

fields.label: The money worry, as it comes to me
The facts I actually know (numbers, dates, who I owe)
The facts I have been avoiding finding out
The decisions that are mine to make
The feelings underneath (shame, fear, anger, grief)
One small step this week
Who I could talk to about the practical side

title: Loneliness Action Plan
summary: A week of small, specific moves toward people, chosen from the client's own life rather than from advice.
goal: Turn a vague wish for more connection into three concrete contacts this week.
body_md: Start from the map of who is already there, however thin, before inventing new groups. Contacts should be small and specific: a message, a coffee, showing up at the same place twice. Plan for the anxiety that arrives before each one, and treat the plan as an experiment to review, not a test to pass.

fields.label: People I already know who I have let drift
Places I go where the same faces appear
Three contacts I will make this week (who, how, when)
What my mind says will happen
What actually happened
Something I could join where I would see the same people weekly
The contact I will repeat next week

title: Session Goals Tracker
summary: Two or three goals set at the start of therapy, rated each session, with a note on what moved them.
goal: Keep the work pointed at what the client came for and make progress visible to both of you.
body_md: Set the goals in the first sessions in the client's words and keep them to three. Rate them briefly at the start of each session; the rating matters less than the conversation about what moved it. Revisit and rewrite the goals when they stop fitting, which is itself progress worth noting.

fields.label: Goal one, in my words
Goal two
Goal three
Today's ratings (0-10 for each)
What moved a rating this week, up or down
A goal that no longer fits, and what would replace it

title: Thought-Feeling-Behavior Triangle
summary: A triangle with a recent situation's thoughts, feelings and actions at the corners, and arrows showing how each fed the others.
goal: Teach the basic CBT model on the client's own example rather than an abstract one.
body_md: Use it in the first sessions, drawn large, with a mild recent example. The arrows are the teaching: ask which corner the client could most easily change, since that is where the work will start. Keep the drawing and refer back to it whenever the model is needed again.

fields.label: The situation
What went through my mind
What I felt (emotions, and in my body)
What I did
Which corner fed which (draw the arrows)
The corner I could most easily change next time

title: Catastrophe Scale
summary: A 0 to 100 scale of bad events, with the client's current worry placed among them.
goal: Restore a sense of proportion by putting the feared outcome next to genuinely worse ones.
body_md: Have the client fill the top of the scale with the worst things they can imagine happening to anyone, then the middle, then place the current worry. Most worries land far lower than they felt. The point is not to dismiss the worry but to size it; ask what the client would do if it actually happened.

fields.label: The worst things I can imagine (90-100)
Very bad things (60-80)
Bad but survivable things (20-50)
Where my current worry sits, honestly
Where it felt like it sat before I did this
What I would actually do if it happened

title: Belief Cost-Benefit Sheet
summary: Weighs what a long-held belief does for the client against what it costs, before deciding whether to challenge it.
goal: Build motivation to loosen a belief by examining its usefulness rather than its truth.
body_md: Useful when a belief is obviously unhelpful but feels true, since arguing truth goes nowhere. Take the benefits seriously; beliefs like I must always be strong have kept the client going. The costs column is where the client's own motivation appears. Finish with a modified version to try, not a rejection.

fields.label: The belief, in my words
What it has done for me
What it costs me
What it costs the people around me
How much I believe it (0-100%)
A modified version I could try this week

title: Coping Statements Card
summary: A pocket card of short, believable statements for the moments the client most often loses their footing.
goal: Give the client rehearsed words for the moment, written while calm.
body_md: The statements must be believable to the client, not cheerful; this has happened before and passed beats everything is fine. Write them for specific moments the client names. Read them aloud in session so the client has heard their own voice say them. Review after a week and cut any that felt false in the moment.

fields.label: The moments I most need something to say to myself
A statement for each, believable to me
What I say to myself now in those moments
The statement I will keep on my phone lock screen
Which statements held up this week, and which felt false

title: Mastery and Pleasure Ratings
summary: A day's activities rated for the sense of achievement and the enjoyment each one gave.
goal: Show the client that achievement and enjoyment come from different activities, and that both are already present in small amounts.
body_md: Rate mastery and pleasure separately for each activity, on a scale that makes small values visible. Clients with low mood typically find that mastery is present in things they discounted as chores. Use the results to plan a week with a deliberate balance rather than defaulting to what feels urgent.

fields.label: Date
Activity (hour by hour, or the main ones)
Mastery: sense of achievement (0-10)
Pleasure: enjoyment (0-10)
The activity with the most surprising rating
What I will add next week for mastery
What I will add for pleasure

title: Sweet Spot Exercise
summary: The client recalls a moment of real vitality in detail and draws out the values it reveals.
goal: Find values through a lived moment rather than a list.
body_md: Ask for a moment, recent or old, when life felt rich, and let the client describe it sense by sense while you listen for the values inside it. Reflect them back as qualities of action, not as feelings. In groups, pairs can interview each other. Follow with one small action this week that carries the same quality.

fields.label: The moment, described in detail
What I was doing, and who was there
What made it matter
The qualities I was living out (curiosity, care, courage, play)
Where those qualities are missing in my week now
One small action this week with the same quality

title: Expansion Practice
summary: A four-step guided practice for making room for a difficult feeling in the body: observe, breathe, allow, expand.
goal: Help the client hold a feeling without fighting it, so it can move.
body_md: Guide it slowly with a feeling of moderate strength the client brings in. Observe the sensation's location and edges, breathe into and around it, allow it to be there, and imagine space opening around it. The client is not trying to make the feeling go; if it changes, note that as a bonus. Record the practice for home use.

fields.label: The feeling I brought to this
Where it sits in my body, and its size and shape
What breathing into it was like
What allowing it was like
What happened as I made room
When I will use this in the week

title: Quicksand Metaphor Sheet
summary: Explores the metaphor of struggling in quicksand: the harder the fight, the deeper the sink.
goal: Help the client see how struggling with a feeling makes it worse, and what lying back would look like.
body_md: Tell the metaphor plainly: in quicksand, the survival move is to spread out and lie back, which is the opposite of what instinct says. Then ask what the client's struggling looks like and what lying back would mean for their feeling. Do not over-explain; let the client make the link.

fields.label: The feeling I keep struggling with
What my struggling looks like (fighting it, escaping it, analyzing it)
What happens to the feeling when I struggle
What lying back would look like for me
What my mind says will happen if I stop struggling
One place I will try lying back this week

title: Kind Hand Practice
summary: A brief self-compassion practice of placing a hand where the pain is and sending warmth through it.
goal: Give the client a physical, wordless way to be kind to themselves in a hard moment.
body_md: Do it in session first, with a feeling of moderate intensity. The client places a hand on the chest, stomach or wherever the feeling sits and lets warmth flow from the hand, as they would for a hurt child. Some clients find it awkward or even unbearable at first; that response is worth exploring gently rather than pushing past.

fields.label: Where I placed my hand
What it was like to do this for myself
What came up that I did not expect
What I would say to a friend in this moment, and whether I could say it to myself
When I will use this in the week

title: Dropping Anchor Practice
summary: A three-step grounding practice for emotional storms: acknowledge what is here, come back into the body, engage with the world.
goal: Give the client a way to steady themselves in a storm without waiting for it to pass.
duration: 5 minutes to teach, then in the moment
body_md: Explain that an anchor does not make the storm go away; it holds you steady until it passes. Run it in session with a real feeling: name what is present, press feet into the floor and stretch, then notice five things in the room. Keep it to a minute or two so it fits real life, and repeat until it is a habit.

fields.label: Acknowledge: what is showing up in me right now (thoughts, feelings, sensations)
Come back: what I did with my body (feet, hands, breath, stretch)
Engage: five things I noticed in the room
What changed, and what did not
A storm this week where I dropped anchor

title: Mindfulness What and How Log
summary: A daily record of one mindful activity, noting which what skill and which how skill were used.
goal: Turn the DBT mindfulness skills from a list into a daily practice with specific instances.
body_md: The what skills are observe, describe, participate; the how skills are non-judgmentally, one-mindfully, effectively. Have the client pick one of each per day and apply them to something ordinary like washing up or walking. The judgment column is where most clients discover how much commentary runs alongside their day.

fields.label: Date and the activity
What skill I used (observe, describe, participate)
How skill I used (non-judgmentally, one-mindfully, effectively)
Judgments I noticed and let go of
How long I stayed with it before drifting
What I will try tomorrow

title: Validation Levels Practice
summary: Rewrites a recent reply to someone as a validating response, working up through the levels.
goal: Teach the client to validate others, and themselves, as a skill rather than an instinct.
body_md: Use a recent exchange where the client felt the conversation go wrong. Work up the levels: paying attention, reflecting back, reading the unspoken, validating in terms of history, validating in terms of the present, and radical genuineness. Then turn the same sheet inward on something the client has been invalidating in themselves.

fields.label: What the other person said or did
What I actually replied
A reply that shows I was paying attention
A reply that reflects back what they said
A reply that makes sense of their reaction given their history or the situation
Something in myself I have been dismissing, and a validating sentence for it

title: Dialectical Thinking Sheet
summary: Takes an either-or judgment and finds the both-and that holds two truths at once.
goal: Loosen black-and-white thinking by practicing the middle path on real examples.
body_md: Start with the client's own either-or statements: I am a failure or a success, they love me or they do not. Write the two truths side by side and join them with and rather than but. Model it in session with your own example. The doing prompt matters, since a dialectic that changes nothing is just a slogan.

fields.label: An either-or judgment I have made this week
The truth on one side
The truth on the other side
Both together, joined with and
What changes in how I feel when I hold both
What I could do differently now that I hold both

title: Willing Hands Practice
summary: A body posture of open, upturned hands practiced during moments of resistance or anger.
goal: Change the emotion by changing the body, when the mind will not budge.
body_md: Teach it alongside half-smile: arms relaxed, hands open and palms up, whether standing, sitting or lying down. Practice with a mildly irritating memory and notice the shift, then assign it to real moments in the week. Clients often find the posture itself feels like giving in; that reaction is the willfulness the skill is for.

fields.label: When I tried it in session, and what I noticed
The moments this week I most need it
What my hands were doing before
What happened when I turned them over
Where I used it this week, and the number before and after (0-10)

title: Model of Emotions Worksheet
summary: Traces one emotion through the model: prompting event, interpretation, body response, urge, action and aftereffects.
goal: Show the client the parts of an emotion so any part can become a place to intervene.
body_md: Pick a recent emotion of moderate strength and walk it through each box in order. Clients are often surprised by how much of the emotion is interpretation and how much is body. Ask which box a skill could go into; that decides whether the next step is check the facts, opposite action or self-soothing.

fields.label: The emotion, and its intensity (0-100)
Prompting event
My interpretation of it
Body sensations and changes
The urge that came with it
What I actually did
The aftereffects (on me, on others, on the next hour)
Which box a skill could go into

title: Intimacy Map
summary: Each partner rates closeness across several kinds of intimacy and says where they would like more.
goal: Widen a couple's idea of intimacy beyond the one kind they are arguing about.
body_md: Cover emotional, physical, intellectual, playful, practical and spiritual intimacy, or whatever set fits the couple. Each rates now and wished-for on each kind, separately, then compare. The gaps that surprise each partner are the material; a couple stuck on one kind usually has another that has quietly worked.

fields.label: Emotional closeness: now and wished-for (0-10)
Physical closeness: now and wished-for
Playfulness together: now and wished-for
Shared interests and conversation: now and wished-for
Practical teamwork: now and wished-for
The kind I most want more of, and what one step would look like
The kind that is quietly working, and what keeps it going

title: Household Fairness Audit
summary: Each partner lists the household work they do, including the noticing and planning, before comparing lists.
goal: Make the whole load visible so fairness can be discussed with facts instead of impressions.
body_md: Lists are written separately and include the invisible work: remembering, anticipating, scheduling, deciding. Read them aloud without defending or correcting. Fairness is not necessarily fifty-fifty; the aim is that both feel the split is agreed rather than assumed. Choose one shift to try for a month.

fields.label: Everything I do around the house, including the thinking work
What I did not know my partner did
What I would like taken off my plate
What I could take on
Where our sense of what is fair differs
One shift we agree to try this month

title: Apology Language Sheet
summary: Each partner spells out what an apology needs to contain for it to land with them.
goal: Stop apologies bouncing off because each partner is apologizing the way they would want to receive one.
body_md: Ask each partner for an apology that worked and one that did not, and pull out the ingredients: naming the hurt, taking responsibility, regret, repair, a plan. Partners often differ on which ingredient is essential. Rehearse one apology each in session, in the other's language.

fields.label: An apology I received that actually worked, and why
One that did not, and what was missing
What an apology needs to contain for me, in order of importance
What makes an apology worse for me (excuses, but, over-apologizing)
My partner's ingredients, as I understood them
An apology I owe, written in their language

title: Individual and Shared Goals Sheet
summary: Each partner names personal goals for the year, then the couple names shared ones and how each will support the other's.
goal: Keep each partner's own growth alive inside the relationship instead of in competition with it.
body_md: Individual goals come first and are not negotiated, only heard. Shared goals are built together. The support prompts are where the sheet earns its place: what each needs from the other to pursue their own goal, said out loud. Revisit at the half year.

fields.label: My own goals for this year
What I need from my partner to pursue them
My partner's goals, as I heard them
How I will support them
Our shared goals
The first shared step, and who does what
When we will check in on all of this

title: Stress Signatures Sheet
summary: Each partner describes how stress shows up in them and what actually helps, so the other can read the signs.
goal: Replace guessing and taking it personally with a shared guide to each partner's stress.
body_md: Each partner writes their own signature: the early signs, the unhelpful things they do, what helps and what makes it worse. Then swap and read. Most couples discover that the thing one does to help is the thing the other finds worst. Agree a signal for I am stressed, not angry at you.

fields.label: The early signs that I am stressed (body, mood, habits)
What I tend to do when stressed that is not helpful
What actually helps me
What makes it worse, even if it is well meant
