Agree a two-minute review with two questions only: what actually happened, and what would a kind observer say. Then a physical switch. Practice on the last event the client replayed.

fields.label: The event I keep replaying
What I replay most (a sentence, a look, a pause)
My two-minute review: what actually happened
What a kind observer would say
My switch when the two minutes are up
How long the replay used to last, and how long it lasted this time

title: Social Prediction Log
summary: Records the client's forecast before a social situation and the outcome after, to compare over weeks.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that their predictions run far worse than events.
body_md: The forecast must be specific and rated: they will notice me blushing and think less of me, seventy percent. Afterward the client records what observably happened, not how it felt. Review the gap across ten entries, which is usually where belief shifts rather than in any single event.

fields.label: The upcoming situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
What observably happened
How I know (what people said or did)
How the prediction compared
What I predict next time, adjusted

title: Conversation Toolkit Card
summary: A pocket card of openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits for social situations.
goal: Reduce the load of inventing conversation so the client can practice being in it.
body_md: Build it with the client's own words, not scripts from a book, and include exits, since knowing they can leave makes staying easier. Warn against using it as a safety behavior: the card is for learning, and the goal is to need it less. Rehearse a full opener-question-exit in session.

fields.label: Three openers I could actually say
Three follow-up questions that work in most conversations
Two ways to leave a conversation gracefully
What I will do with my hands
The one I will try first this week
How it went, and whether I needed the card

title: Social Brave Steps for Teens
summary: A teen's own ladder of social situations from easy to hard, with a brave step per week.
goal: Give a teenager a graded, self-chosen path back into the social situations they have been dodging.
body_md: Let the teen build and order the steps; a ladder chosen by an adult will not be climbed. Keep parents to a support role agreed on the sheet. Steps should be specific: ask one question in class, not participate more. Celebrate attempts, not outcomes, and expect a step to be repeated before moving up.

fields.label: Situations I have been avoiding
My ladder, easiest at the bottom
This week's step
What I am afraid will happen
What actually happened
What my parent will do (and not do) to help
The step for next week

title: Continuing Bonds Letter
summary: A letter to the person who died, about what has happened since and what the client still carries of them.
goal: Support an ongoing connection with the person rather than a closing of the door.
body_md: Offer it as one option among several, since some clients find writing to the dead unbearable and others find it the only thing that helps. Frame the bond as something that changes rather than ends. The client decides whether to read it aloud, keep it, or take it somewhere. Include 988 among the prompts for the darkest hours.

fields.label: What I want to tell you about since you died
What I have kept of you (a habit, a phrase, an object, a way of seeing)
What I wish I had said
What I think you would say to me now
How I will keep you in my life going forward
If the grief ever gets dangerously dark: 988 (call or text), and who else I will reach

title: Grief Triggers Calendar
summary: A year at a glance with the dates, seasons and events likely to bring the grief up hard.
goal: Let the client see the hard days coming and plan support for them instead of being ambushed.
body_md: Include the obvious dates and the sideways ones: the first snow, the tax season the person used to handle, the song at the store. Plan for the week before an anniversary, which is often worse than the day. Decide with the client who will know about each date.

fields.label: Anniversaries and birthdays
Seasons, holidays and rituals that will be different
Sideways reminders I can predict
The next hard date, and what I will do that day
Who will know it is coming
What helped on the last hard date, and what did not

title: Dual Process Week Planner
summary: A week planned with time for facing the loss and time for the ordinary business of living, both on purpose.
goal: Normalize moving between grief and daily life instead of feeling guilty about either.
body_md: Explain that healthy grief moves between the loss and the rest of life, and that neither side is avoidance. Clients stuck on one side feel guilty when they laugh, or numb when they cannot cry; the planner gives both permission. Keep the entries small and concrete.

fields.label: Times this week I will let myself be with the loss (looking at photos, visiting, talking about them)
Times this week I will do ordinary or even pleasant things
The side I tend to get stuck on
What guilt says when I switch sides
What I will say back to it
How the week went

title: Memory Box Project
summary: A child decorates a box and fills it with objects, drawings and stories that hold the person who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a concrete, permitted place for their memories and a way to talk about them.
body_md: Let the child lead on what goes in and what stays private. Each item comes with a story the child tells if they want to; the telling is the work. Involve the surviving parent or carer where possible, and coach them to follow the child's pace rather than their own. Revisit the box on hard dates.

fields.label: What my box looks like
The first three things I put in it, and why
A story that goes with one of them
Something I want to ask about the person who died
Who I can open the box with
When I might want to open it

title: Grief Conversation Cards
summary: A deck of gentle prompts about the person who died, drawn in turn by family members or a group.
goal: Let a family or group talk about the person in a structured, low-pressure way.
body_md: Write the prompts with the group first so nothing on a card ambushes anyone, mixing light ones with heavier ones. Any card can be passed. Play in a circle with a talking object. In families, children often answer more freely than adults, which gives the adults permission.

fields.label: Prompts we put on the cards
The card I drew, and what I said
Something I learned about the person from someone else
A card I passed on
The card I would like to answer next time

title: Needs Inventory for Partners
summary: Each partner lists their needs in the relationship, ranked, and guesses their partner's list before comparing.
goal: Replace assumed needs with stated ones, and show each partner what the other has been guessing.
body_md: Have both partners complete it separately, including the guess about each other, before any discussion. The gaps between the guess and the real list are the material. Keep the tone of curiosity when a partner's need surprises the other; surprise is information, not an accusation.

fields.label: My top five needs in this relationship, ranked
How well each is being met right now (0-10)
What I think my partner's top five are
What surprised me about their real list
One need of theirs I could meet better this month
One need of mine I will ask for directly

title: Perpetual Problems Sorter
summary: Sorts a couple's recurring arguments into the solvable and the perpetual, and plans a different approach to each.
goal: Stop a couple from trying to solve what needs managing, and from managing what could be solved.
body_md: List the arguments first, then sort. Perpetual problems come from differences in personality or values and will be there in ten years; the goal is dialogue and humor about them, not a fix. Solvable problems get a concrete plan. Most couples are relieved to hear that having perpetual problems is normal.

fields.label: Arguments we have more than once a month
Which of these come from a difference in who we are
Which could actually be solved with a plan
For one solvable problem: our plan
For one perpetual problem: what we can each accept
How we will talk about the perpetual one next time it comes up

title: Trust Rebuilding Steps
summary: A shared ladder of specific, observable actions that would rebuild trust after a breach, with a timeline.
goal: Turn a vague demand to earn trust back into steps both partners can see happening.
body_md: The hurt partner names what would help; the other partner says what they can commit to. Steps must be observable, since promises to change are not. Agree how long the checking phase lasts, because trust cannot rebuild under permanent surveillance. Review progress monthly in session.

fields.label: What was broken, in one sentence each
Actions that would help me trust again (specific and visible)
Which of these I can commit to, and when
What transparency looks like for now, and for how long
What I need to hear when I have a wobble
How we will mark progress

title: Communication Pattern Replay
summary: Replays one recent exchange line by line, with each partner naming what they meant and what they heard.
goal: Show a couple the gap between what was said, what was meant and what landed.
body_md: Pick a short exchange, not the biggest fight. Write the actual lines, then have each partner add what they meant and what they heard. The gaps are usually where the fight lives. Finish by rewriting two lines each, and rehearse the rewrite in session.

fields.label: The exchange, line by line, as it happened
For my lines: what I meant
For their lines: what I heard
Where the gap between meant and heard was widest
Two lines I would rewrite
How the rewritten version sounds out loud

title: Relationship Values Compass
summary: Each partner names the kind of partner they want to be, separately from how the other is behaving.
goal: Anchor each partner to their own values so change does not wait on the other person moving first.
body_md: Works with a couple or with one partner alone. The key move is separating my values as a partner from what I get back; clients often discover they have been acting on a scoreboard. Choose one valued action for the week that does not depend on the other person's response.

fields.label: The partner I want to be, in three words
How I have actually been acting lately
What I have been waiting for my partner to do first
One valued action I will take this week regardless
What my mind says will happen if I go first
What actually happened

title: Safety and Stabilization Plan
summary: A plan for the practical and emotional safety a survivor needs in place before any deeper work.
goal: Put steady ground under the client first: who, where, what, and what to do when it gets too much.
body_md: Complete it together in session and never as homework. Cover present-day safety from the person who harmed them, the people who help, the skills that bring them back, and what to do in the worst hours. Move at the client's pace and do not ask for the details of what happened; that is not what this sheet is for. Include 988.

fields.label: Am I safe from the person now? What would make me safer
People I trust, and what each one can help with
Skills that bring me back when I am flooded
Signs that I am doing too much too fast
What I will do in the worst hour: 988 (call or text), and my other numbers
What I want my therapist to know about pace
What I am not ready to talk about yet, and that is fine

title: Consent and Boundaries Map
summary: Maps the client's yes, no and maybe across touch, closeness and conversation, in their own words.
goal: Help a survivor reclaim the right to decide, in small everyday ways, what they allow and what they do not.
body_md: Keep it to everyday boundaries at first: hugs, sitting close, questions from family, who has their number. The maybe column matters, since survivors often feel boundaries must be absolute to count. Rehearse one no in session. Nothing here asks about the abuse itself.

fields.label: Things I am a clear yes to
Things I am a clear no to
Things that are a maybe, and what would make them a yes
A boundary someone in my life keeps crossing
How I will say no to that, in my words
What I will do if they push
Someone who respects my boundaries well

title: Shame Response Sheet
summary: Catches the self-blame that follows abuse, tests it against what the client would say to another survivor, and writes the fairer version.
goal: Loosen the belief that the client caused, allowed or deserved what happened.
body_md: Do this in session, gently, and expect the double standard to be stark: the client will extend to another survivor a compassion they refuse themselves. Do not argue the client out of the belief; let the comparison do the work, and rate belief before and after. Stop if the client becomes flooded and return to grounding.

fields.label: What I tell myself about why it happened
How much I believe that (0-100%)
What I would say to a friend who told me the same story
Where the blame actually belongs
The fairer statement, in my words
How much I believe the fairer statement now (0-100%)

title: Support Disclosure Planner
summary: Plans whether, who, when and how much to tell, so a disclosure happens on the client's terms.
goal: Keep the choice of who knows, and how much, in the survivor's hands.
body_md: Not telling is a valid outcome of this sheet and should be said out loud. Work through what the client wants from telling, who is likely to respond well, and how much to say; a first sentence and an exit line are worth rehearsing. Plan for the reaction being disappointing, since it sometimes is.

fields.label: What I hope telling someone would give me
People I might tell, and how I think each would respond
The person I would tell first, if anyone
How much I want to say (a sentence is enough)
My first sentence
How I will end the conversation if I need to
What I will do for myself afterward, whatever their reaction

title: Body Safety Rules Poster
summary: A child makes a poster of body safety rules: private parts, okay and not-okay touch, secrets versus surprises, and who to tell.
goal: Teach a child the words and the permission to tell, as part of prevention work with families.
body_md: A prevention and education tool, done with a parent in the room where possible. Use correct names for body parts. Teach that surprises are fun and short and secrets about bodies are never kept. List five trusted adults. If a child discloses during this, stop the activity, stay calm, believe them, and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Private parts have proper names, and mine are
Okay touch and not-okay touch: my examples
The difference between a surprise and a secret
My five trusted grown-ups
What I say if someone breaks a body safety rule
Where my poster will hang

title: Coping Menu by Situation
summary: A menu of the client's coping options sorted by where they are: at work, in public, at home, in bed.
goal: Match skills to settings so the right one is available where the distress actually happens.
body_md: Most clients have skills that only work at home and distress that happens elsewhere. Sort by setting and check that each setting has at least two options that are invisible to other people. Include one for the middle of the night. Keep the menu in the phone's notes.

fields.label: At work or school: two things I can do without anyone noticing
In public: two options
At home: two options
In bed at 3 a.m.: two options
The skill I reach for too often, and where it does not work
The new skill I will try this week, and where

title: Skill Practice Log
summary: A weekly log of which coping skill the client used, in what situation, and how well it worked.
goal: Turn coping from a vague resolve into a tracked practice with results.
body_md: The rating is the useful part: a skill that scores three out of ten in three different situations can be retired without guilt. Look for the mismatch between skills tried and situations faced. Praise the attempt, especially when the skill did not work, since trying is what builds the habit.

fields.label: Date and the situation
Distress before (0-10)
The skill I used
Distress after (0-10)
How well it worked (0-10) and why
A skill I could have used instead
The skill I will practice most next week

title: Coping Ladder for Kids
summary: A ladder of a child's coping moves from small feelings at the bottom to big ones at the top.
goal: Match the size of the coping move to the size of the feeling, in a picture a child can use.
body_md: Draw a ladder with three or four rungs and let the child assign feelings sizes to each. Small feelings get small moves: a breath, a drink of water. Big feelings get big moves: a break, a grown-up. Practice one move per rung in session and have the parent post the ladder at home.

fields.label: Bottom rung: a small feeling and my small move
Middle rung: a medium feeling and my medium move
Top rung: a huge feeling and my biggest move
How I know which rung I am on
Who helps me on the top rung
Where my ladder is posted

title: Coping Skills Relay
summary: Teams race to act out or demonstrate a coping skill for each situation card drawn.
goal: Rehearse coping skills under mild pressure and laughter, so they are practiced rather than just known.
body_md: Write situation cards with the group beforehand: a test tomorrow, a friend ignoring a text, a loud house. A team scores when the skill fits the situation and could actually be done there. Judge fit, not speed, and let the group argue the call; the argument is the learning.

fields.label: Situation cards we made
Skills my team demonstrated
A skill another team showed that I want to steal
A situation none of us could match well
The skill I will practice this week

title: Helpful vs Costly Coping Sort
summary: Sorts everything the client does to feel better into what helps in the long run and what costs more than it gives.
goal: Help the client judge coping by its long-term workability rather than by how fast it works.
body_md: List everything without judgment first, including the ones the client is ashamed of; those are usually the fastest-acting. Sort by long-term workability, not by how they look. Most clients find a few things belong in both columns depending on amount, which is worth writing down rather than resolving.

fields.label: Everything I do to feel better, fast or slow
Which ones help me next week too
Which ones cost more than they give
Which ones depend on how much
One costly one I will shrink, and how
One helpful one I will do more of, and when

title: Phobia Prediction Tracker
summary: Records what the client expects to happen around the feared object or situation and what actually occurs.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that the feared outcome and the felt danger diverge.
body_md: Ask for the specific feared outcome, not just fear: I will faint, the dog will bite, the plane will crash. Rate belief before and after each approach. The pattern across entries is what changes belief, so aim for at least eight entries before drawing conclusions together.

fields.label: The feared thing and the situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
Peak fear (0-10)
What actually happened
What I did during the peak
My belief in the prediction now (0-100%)

title: Approach Steps Planner
summary: Plans the next approach step toward a feared object in detail: where, how long, with whom, and what to drop.
goal: Make each approach step concrete enough to actually happen this week.
body_md: One step at a time, planned to the minute. Include what safety moves the client will drop, since carrying the escape plan into the step blunts it. Decide in advance how long to stay: long enough for the fear to fall, not just to touch and run. Debrief in session before planning the next.

fields.label: This week's step
Where and when, exactly
Who will be there, and what they will and will not do
How long I will stay (until fear drops by half)
The safety moves I will not use
What happened, and what I will do next week

title: Phobia Body Response Sheet
summary: Names what the client's body does around the feared thing, and separates the alarm from the danger.
goal: Help the client see the fear response as an alarm that can fire without a fire.
body_md: Map the response: heart, breath, muscles, stomach, the urge to run. Explain plainly that the body's alarm is doing its job and that the job is to get them out, which is why staying feels wrong. For blood or needle fears, note the faint response and plan applied tension separately.

fields.label: What my body does first around the feared thing
What it does next
The urge that comes with it
What the alarm is trying to make me do
What I know about the real danger in this situation
What I will do with the alarm next time it fires

title: Brave Practice Chart for Kids
summary: A sticker chart for a child's repeated brave practices with a feared thing, tied to a small reward.
goal: Make repetition of approach steps visible and rewarding for a child.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then daily
body_md: Choose practices small enough to repeat daily: look at a picture of a dog, stand in the doorway with the lights off. Stickers go on for attempts, not for calm. Parents hold the chart and the reward and keep their own anxiety out of the practice. Change the practice when it stops earning fear.

fields.label: My brave practice this week
Stickers I earned
How scared I was the first time (0-10) and the last time
My reward when the chart is full
What my grown-up does during practice
Next week's brave practice

title: Fear Ladder Card Sort
summary: Situations written on cards and physically sorted into a ladder from least to most scary.
goal: Build a fear hierarchy as a hands-on sorting task rather than a form.
body_md: Write one situation per card with the client, at least fifteen, then sort them on the table or floor. The physical sorting draws out distinctions a form misses, and the client can move cards as beliefs change. Photograph the finished ladder and use it to choose the next approach step.

fields.label: Situations we wrote on cards
The bottom three cards
The top three cards
Cards I moved while sorting, and why
The card I will start with
The card I cannot imagine reaching yet

title: Body Neutrality Practice
summary: Daily short statements about what the body did today rather than how it looked.
goal: Move the client's relationship with their body from judgment toward function and use.
duration: Two minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Aim for neutral, not positive; clients who cannot believe their body is beautiful can believe it carried them up the stairs. Keep the statements about doing and feeling. Notice when the client sneaks an appearance comment in and gently redirect. Never mention weight, shape or food in this practice.

fields.label: Three things my body did for me today
One thing it let me feel (warmth, music, a hug, the wind)
A neutral statement about my body, without judgment either way
What my mind wanted to add about how it looks
How I responded to that
The statement I will use tomorrow morning

title: Body Checking Log
summary: Records the mirror checks, pinching, comparing and photo scrutiny that keep body worry alive, and what each one did to mood.
goal: Show the client how checking feeds the worry, and plan a reduction.
body_md: Checking feels like getting information but produces worse mood almost every time; the log makes that visible. Include the quiet forms: reflections in windows, comparing in group photos, clothes tried and discarded. Plan one check to cut in half, not to stop entirely.

fields.label: Date and time
What I checked, and how (mirror, pinch, photo, comparing)
What I was looking for
Mood before and after (0-10)
How long the reassurance lasted, if any
The check I will cut in half next week
What I will do instead in that moment

title: Appearance Assumptions Sheet
summary: Lists the client's rules linking appearance to worth, acceptance or success, and tests each one.
goal: Loosen the beliefs that make appearance carry the whole weight of self-worth.
body_md: Draw out the if-then rules: if I looked different, then people would... Test each against the client's own experience and the people they admire. The goal is to shrink the share of self-worth that appearance holds, which a pie chart of what makes up their worth can show before and after.

fields.label: My rules about appearance (if I looked..., then...)
Where each rule came from
Evidence from my own life for and against it
People I admire, and how much their looks have to do with it
How much of my self-worth appearance holds now (%)
What else I would like it to rest on

title: Body Gratitude Function List
summary: A list of what the client's body has carried them through, by life stage, written as a record rather than a rating.
goal: Build a history of the body as a companion rather than an object under review.
body_md: Move through life stages: childhood play, illness survived, work done, people carried, places reached. The tone is a record, not a pep talk. Clients with a history of harming or overworking their body may find this tender; slow down there. No comments on shape or size anywhere on the sheet.

fields.label: What my body did for me as a child
What it has carried me through
What it lets me do that I would miss
Someone it has held or helped
Something it recovered from
What I would like to thank it for, plainly

title: Media Diet Audit
summary: An inventory of the accounts, shows and images the client consumes, and what each does to how they feel in their body.
goal: Change what the client feeds their body image, since much of it arrives through a screen.
body_md: Go through the phone together. For each account or habit, ask what it does to the client's body feeling in the ten minutes after. Unfollowing is a real intervention and often the fastest one; replace, do not just remove, so the feed is not empty. Repeat in a month.

fields.label: Accounts and shows I see most
How I feel in my body after each (better, worse, nothing)
The ones that leave me comparing
Accounts I will unfollow or mute this week
What I will follow instead (bodies doing things, other interests entirely)
How my feed feels after the change

title: Character Strengths Checklist
summary: A checklist of strength words a client circles, ranks and backs up with real examples.
goal: Use it to build a shared vocabulary for the strengths a client already has.
body_md: The client scans a list of strength words, circling any that fit, then narrows to a top five and writes one specific recent moment for each rather than a general trait. Some clients rush to modest, vague answers or skip strengths they feel they haven't earned; slow them down and press for a concrete example. Useful as an opener before goal-setting or values work, since it hands the clinician language the client already owns.

fields.label: Circle every strength word below that sounds like you.
From those, pick your top five and put them in order.
Write one specific recent moment you used your top strength.
Which strength do you use so often you forget it counts?
Which strength would you like to use more this month?
Who in your life would agree with this list, and who might be surprised?

title: Boundary Practice Hierarchy
summary: A ranked list of boundary-setting situations from easiest to hardest to practice in order.
goal: Use it to sequence boundary practice so a client builds confidence gradually.
body_md: The client lists situations where they'd like to hold a boundary, then ranks them from easiest to hardest and picks a script for the easiest one to try first. Clients often want to start with the hardest relationship on the list; steer them toward a low-stakes situation so an early success builds momentum. Revisit the ranking each week, moving down the list only after a step feels manageable, and use the sheet to plan what to say and how to handle pushback.

fields.label: List five situations where you wish you set a clearer boundary.
Rank them from easiest (1) to hardest (5) to practice.
Write the exact words you'll use for your easiest one.
What do you expect the other person to say back?
How will you respond if they push back?
After you try it, what actually happened?

title: Habit Stacking Planner
summary: A worksheet that attaches a new habit to a routine the client already does daily.
goal: Use it to help a client anchor a new habit to an existing one instead of relying on willpower.
duration: Five minutes daily for several weeks
body_md: The client names a small habit they already do without thinking, like making coffee or brushing their teeth, and attaches the new habit right after it using an if-then sentence. The most common trip-up is choosing a new habit that's too big or an anchor habit that doesn't happen at a consistent time; help them shrink both. Check in on the stack each week and adjust the anchor or the size of the habit rather than abandoning the idea.

fields.label: What's a small habit you already do every day without thinking?
What new habit do you want to build?
Finish this: After I [anchor habit], I will [new habit].
How will you make the new habit take less than two minutes at first?
What might get in the way this week?
How did the stack go by the end of the week?

title: Listening Skills Self-Check
summary: A self-rating sheet where a client scores their own listening habits in real conversations.
goal: Use it to help a client notice which listening habits help and which ones interrupt.
body_md: The client rates how often they interrupt, plan their reply while the other person is talking, or reflect back what they heard, then picks one habit to work on this week. Clients often rate themselves generously; asking for a specific recent conversation as evidence sharpens the answers. Pair it with a short role-play in session so the clinician can point out what the client's own ratings missed.

fields.label: How often do you interrupt before the other person finishes?
How often are you planning your reply instead of listening?
How often do you check what you heard by repeating it back?
Describe a recent conversation where you listened well.
Describe one where you wish you'd listened differently.
Which listening habit will you practice this week?

title: Stress Curve Psychoeducation Sheet
summary: A diagram showing how performance rises then falls as stress and arousal increase.
goal: Use it to help a client see that some stress helps and too much or too little hurts.
body_md: Walk the client through a simple curve showing performance climbing with mild stress, peaking, then dropping as stress builds further, and ask them to mark where they usually sit day to day. Clients sometimes hear this as permission to chase more stress rather than as a way to notice when they've tipped past their peak; keep the focus on their own signs of tipping over, not a general rule. Use their markings to plan one small change that nudges them back toward the peak.

fields.label: Where on the curve do you usually sit most days?
What does it feel like in your body when you're on the rising side?
What does it feel like when you've tipped past the peak?
What's one sign that tells you you've gone too far?
What's one thing that brings you back down the curve?

title: Anxiety's Job Description Worksheet
summary: Explores what a client believes their anxiety is trying to accomplish for them.
goal: Use it to surface the protective story behind anxiety and weigh its actual payoff.
body_md: Ask the client to write anxiety's 'job description' as if it were an employee: what it thinks its duties are, what it believes would happen if it stopped working so hard, and what it actually costs the client in energy or missed moments. Clients often list only the downsides of anxiety and skip what they believe it protects them from; push gently for both sides. Use the finished sheet to open a conversation about which duties still feel needed and which could be handed off or scaled back.

fields.label: If anxiety had a job title, what would it be?
What does anxiety believe would happen if it stopped doing this job?
What does this job cost you day to day?
Which part of this job feels like it could be scaled back?
What would you do with the energy anxiety is currently spending?

title: Minimum Viable Day Planner
summary: Lays out the smallest version of a day a client can still call a win.
goal: Use it to lower the bar on low-energy days without abandoning structure entirely.
body_md: Work with the client to list the smallest possible version of each daily task, such as a two-minute shower instead of a full routine, so there is always a version they can complete on a low day. Clients often set the minimum version too high out of habit; keep pushing it smaller until they visibly relax about it. Use the sheet on genuinely hard mornings rather than every day, and review afterward whether the minimum version still counted as something worth noticing.

fields.label: List three tasks you usually do in a day.
What is the smallest possible version of each one?
Which minimum version did you complete today?
How did it feel to do the smaller version instead of skipping it?
What would make tomorrow's minimum version even easier to start?

title: Life Beyond Substance Use Sheet
summary: Maps the roles, activities, and people that exist apart from substance use.
goal: Use it to widen a client's sense of identity beyond substance use and urges.
body_md: Have the client list roles, activities, and relationships that matter to them and are not organized around substance use, then rate how much attention each currently gets. Clients in early recovery often find this list thinner than expected, which is useful information rather than a failure. Use the sheet to pick one under-attended area to invest a small amount of time in this week, and revisit it periodically as the list of what matters outside urges naturally grows.

fields.label: List three roles or relationships that matter to you.
List two activities you enjoy that have nothing to do with substance use.
How much attention has each one gotten lately, 0 to 10?
Which one would you like to invest a little more time in this week?
What is one small step toward that this week?

title: Anger Trigger Stack Worksheet
summary: Tracks the small stressors that pile up before a single anger blow-up.
goal: Use it to make the buildup before an outburst visible, not just the final trigger.
body_md: Have the client walk back through a recent anger episode and list every small stressor that stacked up beforehand, not just the final straw, noting roughly how full the stack felt at each point on a scale. Clients often can only name the last trigger; use guided questions about the hours before to surface the earlier layers. Once the stack is visible, identify one layer that could be unloaded earlier next time, such as a break or a boundary, well before the stack gets close to full.

fields.label: What was the final trigger right before the anger episode?
List the smaller stressors from earlier that day.
How full did the stack feel at each point, 0 to 10?
Which layer could you unload earlier next time?
What would unloading it look like in the moment?

title: Compulsion Function Log
summary: Tracks what each ritual actually relieves, not just how long it takes.
goal: Use it to map what a ritual quiets so exposure work targets the right worry.
body_md: Have the client log each ritual for a week, noting the trigger, the specific worry it seems to quiet, and how long relief lasts before the urge returns; most people are surprised to see one or two worries driving several different rituals, which helps target exposure and response prevention work instead of chasing every compulsion at once.

fields.label: What happened right before I felt the urge?
What ritual did I do?
What worry was I trying to quiet?
How long did the relief last?
What would have happened if I hadn't done it?

title: Positive Attention Ratio Tracker
summary: Counts positive comments against corrections across an ordinary day.
goal: Use it to rebalance a day that has drifted toward mostly correcting a child.
body_md: Have the parent make two simple tallies through one ordinary day, one for comments that noticed something good and one for corrections, warnings, or commands; use the ratio as a plain baseline for later work rather than a verdict on the parent, since most parents are startled by how lopsided the count turns out to be.

fields.label: Tally: things I said that noticed something good.
Tally: corrections, warnings, or commands I gave.
What surprised me about the count?
What is one moment today I could have narrated positively instead?

title: New Parent Support Needs Inventory
summary: Sorts what kind of help a new parent actually needs by category.
goal: Use it to turn a vague need for help into requests others can act on.
body_md: Have the client list needs across practical tasks, emotional support, information, and time alone, then name a specific person for each rather than leaving it as a general wish for more help; this pairs well with a later partner conversation, and clients often stall not at listing needs but at naming who to actually ask.

fields.label: Practical tasks I need help with right now.
Emotional support I need right now.
Information or reassurance I need right now.
Who could I actually ask for each of these?
What is stopping me from asking?

title: Pre-Event Body Signal Checklist
summary: Catalogs the physical warning signs that show up before a social event.
goal: Use it to help someone recognize their own pattern of anticipatory signals.
body_md: Have the client check off which physical signals typically appear in the hours before a social event, such as a tight stomach, rehearsing lines, or repeated mirror checks, and rate each one across a few events; the same one or two signals usually show up earliest and most reliably, which can become a cue to use a coping skill rather than a reason to cancel.

fields.label: Which body signals show up before a social event?
Rate each one from mild to strong.
Which signal shows up earliest, most reliably?
What could that early signal remind me to do?

title: Secondary Losses Inventory
summary: Maps the smaller losses that ripple out from a single death or ending.
goal: Use it to help a client name what else changed besides the loss itself.
body_md: Hand this to a client who feels stuck on one big loss without noticing everything that shifted around it — a routine, a role, a sense of safety, a social circle. Walk through each life area together and list what quietly went missing too. Clients often name only the person or thing lost at first; give them time and prompts to notice the secondary losses, since naming them can explain why grief feels bigger than the loss alone. Watch for a client who uses this to catalog blame rather than loss.

fields.label: One loss I can name right away is…
A daily routine that changed because of this loss is…
A role I used to have that feels different now is…
A sense of safety or certainty I lost along with this is…
A relationship or connection that shifted because of this loss is…
The smallest change I've noticed that still catches me off guard is…

title: Autonomy and Togetherness Balance Sheet
summary: Maps how much separateness and closeness each partner wants right now.
goal: Use it to help a client see where their needs for space and closeness diverge from a partner's.
body_md: Have the client plot, on a simple scale, how much time alone versus together they want in a typical week, then guess where they think their partner would plot it, and compare notes afterward if both partners complete it. Differences here are common and not a verdict on the relationship; the point is naming the gap out loud instead of each partner privately deciding the other wants too much or too little. Watch for a client who fills this out defensively, trying to prove they are the reasonable one rather than describe their actual preference.

fields.label: On a typical week, the amount of time alone I want is…
The amount of time together I want is…
Where I think my partner would place their own numbers…
A time recently when this gap showed up between us…
One small adjustment I could make this week…

title: Coping Swap Ladder
summary: Ranks unhelpful coping habits next to an easier and a harder helpful swap.
goal: Use it to help a client find a realistic first step away from an unhelpful habit.
body_md: List the client's go-to unhelpful coping habits down one side, then for each one brainstorm two swaps: an easy one they could try today and a harder one for later, ranked by difficulty rather than treated as an all-or-nothing switch. Clients often reach straight for the hardest swap and then feel like a failure when it doesn't stick; steer them toward the easy swap first and let the ladder show progress over time. Revisit the ladder every few sessions to move entries up as easier swaps become automatic.

fields.label: An unhelpful habit I turn to under stress…
An easier helpful swap I could try today…
A harder helpful swap for later…
What usually gets in the way of trying the swap…
One thing that would make the easy swap more likely…

title: Anticipation Countdown Tracker
summary: Logs dread levels in the days leading up to a planned exposure or feared event.
goal: Use it to show a client how anticipatory dread moves compared to the event itself.
body_md: Before a planned exposure step or an unavoidable feared event, have the client rate their dread once a day counting down, then rate it again right after the event happens. Most clients are surprised to see dread peak well before the event and drop faster afterward than expected; use the chart to make that pattern visible rather than just telling them about it. Watch for a client who avoids logging on the hardest days, which itself is useful information about avoidance patterns.

fields.label: The event or exposure step I'm counting down to…
Three days before: dread level, 0 to 10…
One day before: dread level, 0 to 10…
The morning of: dread level, 0 to 10…
Right after: dread level, 0 to 10…
What I notice comparing the numbers…

title: SMART Goal Builder
summary: A step-by-step sheet that turns a vague goal into a specific, measurable plan.
goal: Use it to help a client turn a wish into a goal they can actually track.
body_md: The client takes one goal and rewrites it against five prompts, specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, until it reads as a concrete plan rather than a wish. Clients often keep the goal too broad, such as be less stressed, or set a deadline with no way to check progress; push for a number or an observable sign. Once the goal is sharpened, use it as the anchor for weekly check-ins on progress.

fields.label: What's the vague version of your goal right now?
What exactly will be different when you reach it?
How will you measure or notice progress along the way?
Is this goal realistic for you in this stretch of time?
Why does this goal matter to you right now?
What's your target date?

title: Barriers and Bridges Planner
summary: A worksheet that pairs each barrier to a goal with a specific bridge past it.
goal: Use it to turn a stuck goal into a list of concrete next moves.
body_md: The client lists what's actually getting in the way of a goal, then writes one specific bridge, a person, a resource, or a small action, next to each barrier. Clients tend to name barriers that are really feelings, like I'm too tired, rather than obstacles they can act on; help them separate the feeling from the concrete blocker underneath it. Revisit the bridges weekly and swap out any that turned out not to work.

fields.label: What goal do you want to make progress on?
List every barrier standing in the way, big or small.
Next to each barrier, write one bridge that could get you past it.
Which bridge can you try first, this week?
Who could help you build one of these bridges?

title: Habit Trigger Chain Log
summary: A log that maps what comes right before and right after a habit the client wants to change.
goal: Use it to find the trigger and payoff that keep an unwanted habit going.
body_md: Each time the habit happens, the client logs what happened just before it, the habit itself, and what happened right after, looking for a repeating trigger and a repeating payoff. Clients often log the habit but skip the moments right before it, since those feel too ordinary to write down; remind them the boring lead-up is usually the trigger. Once a pattern shows up, use the log to test changing the trigger rather than fighting the habit head-on.

fields.label: What happened right before the habit, in the ten minutes prior?
Describe the habit itself: what did you do?
What happened right after, and how did it feel?
What time of day and place does this keep happening?
Looking at a week of entries, what's the repeating trigger?

title: Decision Matrix Scorecard
summary: A scoring grid that weighs each option in a decision against the client's own criteria.
goal: Use it to help a client compare options on paper instead of going in circles.
body_md: The client lists the options they're weighing down one side and the criteria that matter to them across the top, then scores each option against each criterion before totaling the columns. Clients sometimes pick criteria that all point the same direction, which just confirms what they already lean toward; ask what a criterion from the other side of the decision would be. The total score is a starting point for discussion, not the final answer.

fields.label: What decision are you trying to make?
List every option you're seriously considering.
What matters to you in this decision? List three to five criteria.
Score each option from 1 to 5 on each criterion.
Which option came out highest, and does that surprise you?

title: Emotion Granularity Ladder
summary: A ladder that moves a client from a vague feeling word to a more specific one.
goal: Use it to build the emotional vocabulary a client needs for accurate thought records.
body_md: Starting from a vague word like bad or fine, the client climbs a ladder of more specific feeling words until they land on one that actually fits the moment, then names what in the body or situation points to that word. Clients often stop at the second rung because it's already more specific than they're used to; encourage one more step before settling. A richer vocabulary here makes later thought records and check-ins far more precise.

fields.label: Start with the vague word you'd normally use: how are you feeling?
Climb one step: what's a more specific word for that?
Climb again: is there an even more precise word?
What in your body or the situation points to that word?
How intense is that feeling right now, from 0 to 10?

title: External Focus Attention Shift Sheet
summary: Trains a client to deliberately shift attention outward instead of scanning for threat.
goal: Use it to build a repeatable skill for redirecting attention away from internal threat monitoring.
body_md: In session, have the client notice how much attention is on internal sensations or worry versus the outside world, then practice deliberately naming external details for sixty seconds while anxious. Clients often insist they cannot look away from the internal alarm; normalize the pull back inward and count each return to external focus as a rep, not a failure. Use real anxious moments between sessions as practice rounds and log how attention shifted the felt intensity, even briefly.

fields.label: Before the practice: where is most of your attention right now, inside or outside?
Name five things you can see in as much detail as possible.
After the practice: how intense does the anxious feeling feel now, 0 to 10?
What pulled your attention back inward, if anything?
When could you practice this again this week?

title: Hopelessness Evidence Log
summary: Weighs evidence for and against a hopeless prediction across a real week.
goal: Use it to test a hopeless thought against what actually happens, day by day.
body_md: Have the client write down one specific hopeless prediction, such as 'nothing will get better,' then log daily evidence that supports or complicates it. Clients often log only confirming evidence out of habit; prompt them each day for at least one small counter-example, even a minor one. Review the log together at the next session rather than letting the client score it alone, since low mood tends to discount small positives before they get written down.

fields.label: Write the hopeless thought exactly as it shows up for you.
Today's evidence that supports this thought.
Today's evidence that complicates or contradicts this thought.
How strongly do you believe the thought right now, 0 to 100?
What's one thing you noticed today that you almost didn't count?

title: Task-Switch Cost Log
summary: Tracks how much time and focus is lost each time a client switches tasks.
goal: Use it to make the hidden cost of task-switching visible and countable.
body_md: Have the client jot down every time they switch from one task to another before finishing it, noting roughly how long it took to refocus afterward. Clients often underestimate how often this happens until they see it logged over a few days. Review the log together looking for patterns, such as a specific time of day or a specific trigger like a notification, and use it to pick one switching point worth experimenting with first rather than trying to fix all of them at once.

fields.label: What task were you working on before the switch?
What pulled your attention away?
About how long did it take to get back to the first task?
What time of day did this happen?
Which switching point would you like to experiment with first?

title: Anger Intensity Reality Check
summary: Compares a client's in-the-moment anger rating to the situation's actual stakes.
goal: Use it to recalibrate anger intensity ratings against the actual size of the situation.
body_md: Have the client rate how angry a recent situation made them feel, then separately rate how big a deal the situation actually was on the same scale, and compare the gap. A wide gap is the useful finding, not a reason for the client to feel bad; use it to explore what inflated the rating, such as a past pattern or an assumption about intent. Repeat across a few situations to look for a consistent gap size, which can become an early cue the client learns to catch mid-episode.

fields.label: Describe the situation briefly.
How angry did you feel, 0 to 10?
How big a deal was the situation actually, 0 to 10?
What might explain the gap between the two numbers?
What could remind you to check this gap in the moment?

title: Mental Compulsion Spotting Guide
summary: Helps someone tell silent mental rituals apart from ordinary thinking.
goal: Use it to catch mental reviewing, counting, or rewording hiding as thoughts.
body_md: Walk through this checklist of common mental rituals with the client, since many people don't realize replaying a conversation, silently repeating a phrase, or mentally reviewing an action is a compulsion rather than just thinking; do the first pass together in session, because spotting the pattern often takes a second set of eyes before the client can catch it on their own.

fields.label: I replay a conversation in my head until it feels right.
I silently repeat a word or phrase to myself.
I mentally review what I did to check I did it correctly.
I count in my head until reaching a certain number.
I mentally cancel out a bad thought with a good one.

title: Intentional Misbehavior Attribution Check
summary: Tests the automatic thought that a child is misbehaving on purpose.
goal: Use it to separate what a child did from why the parent assumes they did it.
body_md: Have the parent record an incident, the intention they assumed behind it, and at least one other plausible explanation such as tiredness, a developmental stage, or limit-testing, then imagine how they would have reacted believing the other explanation instead; watch for a parent who resists any explanation that doesn't involve deliberate blame.

fields.label: What did my child do?
What did I assume it meant about their intentions toward me?
What is another explanation, even if it's less satisfying?
How would I have responded if I believed the other explanation?

title: Postpartum Social Comparison Log
summary: Catches thoughts sparked by comparing a hard day to someone else's highlight reel.
goal: Use it to test comparison thoughts against what a new parent can actually know.
body_md: Have the client log the comparison moment, often while scrolling, the thought about their own adequacy that followed, and what they genuinely cannot know about the other person's day; reducing exposure to the trigger is a fair option to raise too, not just challenging the thought, and watch for the log itself becoming another reason to keep dwelling on the images.

fields.label: What did I see or compare myself to?
What did I think about myself in that moment?
What don't I actually know about their day?
What would I say to a friend who had this same thought?

title: Discounting the Positive Catch Sheet
summary: Catches the moment someone waves off a compliment or a win as not counting.
goal: Use it to interrupt the habit of dismissing positive evidence about oneself.
body_md: Have the client log a moment they brushed off good feedback or an accomplishment, the exact phrase they used to make it not count, such as anyone could have done that, and what a more balanced read of the same event would sound like; watch for the client agreeing with the balanced read intellectually while still not letting the credit actually land.

fields.label: What positive thing happened or was said to me?
What did I tell myself right after, to make it not count?
What would I say if a friend dismissed the same thing about themselves?
What is a more balanced read of what happened?

title: Meaning Reconstruction Log
summary: Tracks small moments where a client makes new sense of life after a loss.
goal: Use it to help a client notice meaning forming alongside grief, not instead of it.
body_md: Give this to a client several weeks into grieving, once acute waves have started to space out, to log moments — even brief ones — where they find a new way of understanding their loss or their life without the person. This is not about arriving at a tidy silver lining; some entries may stay unresolved, and that is fine. Clients sometimes worry that finding any meaning means the loss did not matter, so name that tension directly and let the log hold both grief and growth side by side.

fields.label: Today I noticed this small moment of understanding or meaning…
What this moment tells me about how I'm making sense of the loss…
A thought I had that still doesn't make sense to me…
Something I believe differently now than before this loss…
A way I've honored or carried forward something from the person or thing I lost…

title: Unmet Expectations Cost-Benefit Sheet
summary: Weighs the cost and benefit of holding on to an unspoken expectation of a partner.
goal: Use it to help a client decide whether to voice, adjust, or release an expectation.
body_md: Use this when a client is quietly resentful about an expectation of their partner that was never actually stated out loud. Have them name the expectation, then list what holding onto it silently costs them and what, if anything, it gets them, followed by the same two columns for voicing it directly instead. Clients often discover the silent version costs more than they realized once it's written down side by side. This works well paired with a plan for how and when to actually voice the expectation, which the clinician can build with the client separately.

fields.label: The expectation of my partner I've never said out loud…
What staying silent about it costs me…
What staying silent about it gets me, if anything…
What voicing it directly might cost me…
What voicing it directly might get me…
What I want to do with this expectation now…

title: Nothing Helps Belief Check
summary: Gathers evidence against the thought that no coping skill ever works.
goal: Use it to test the all-or-nothing belief that coping skills are pointless.
body_md: Use this when a client dismisses coping skills work with a blanket thought like 'nothing helps anyway.' Write the thought down, then go skill by skill through ones they have tried, rating how much each one helped on a 0 to 10 scale rather than a pass-or-fail. Most clients find at least partial relief somewhere once they are asked to rate rather than judge; the point is loosening the all-or-nothing belief, not proving every skill works perfectly. Watch for a client who rates everything a zero reflexively — slow down and ask about a specific recent moment instead of a general impression.

fields.label: The thought I have about coping skills in general…
A skill I've tried: how much did it help, 0 to 10…
A second skill I've tried: how much did it help, 0 to 10…
A third skill I've tried: how much did it help, 0 to 10…
What I notice about the belief now that I've rated these…

title: Predicted vs Actual Fear Outcome Log
summary: Compares a client's predicted worst outcome to what actually happened after facing a fear.
goal: Use it to build evidence against overestimated danger from a specific feared object.
body_md: Before an approach step, have the client write down their specific predicted outcome and how certain they feel about it, then fill in what actually happened right after. Repeating this across several approach steps builds a running record the client can review when facing the next one, which tends to land better than a single conversation about probability. Watch for predictions written vaguely enough to always seem 'sort of' true; push for a specific, checkable prediction each time.

fields.label: The feared object or situation I'm approaching…
My specific predicted outcome…
How certain I am this will happen, 0 to 100%…
What actually happened…
How certain I am now for next time…

title: Before and After Scrolling Belief Test
summary: Tests a client's prediction about mood before and after a specific stretch of scrolling.
goal: Use it to test whether a block of social media time changes mood the way a client expects.
body_md: Before the client opens a social media app for a set block of time, have them write a specific prediction about how they'll feel about their own appearance afterward, and how confident they are in it. Right after, they rate their actual mood and appearance-related thoughts and compare the two. Repeating this across a few apps or accounts often shows some sources reliably worsen mood while others barely register, which lands better than a general talk about screen habits. Watch for vague predictions; push for a specific, checkable one each time.

fields.label: The app or account and time block I'm about to scroll through…
My prediction: how will I feel about my appearance afterward…
How confident I am in that prediction, 0 to 100%…
What I actually felt afterward…
What I noticed comparing the two…

title: 80th Birthday Toast Practice
summary: A guided imagery exercise where a client imagines the toast given at their 80th birthday.
goal: Use it to surface a client's values by imagining how they'd want to be remembered.
body_md: Guide the client to imagine sitting at their own 80th birthday party, listening to someone who knows them well give a toast, and have them write what they'd genuinely want that toast to say. Clients sometimes write what they think they should want rather than what they actually value; ask them to notice if any line feels borrowed from someone else's expectations. Use the toast to name two or three values to build committed action around.

fields.label: Who is giving the toast, and what is your relationship to them?
What do you most want them to say about how you treated people?
What do you want them to say about what you did with your time?
Read your toast back: does any line feel borrowed rather than yours?
What value shows up most clearly in what you wrote?

title: Sing the Thought Defusion Exercise
summary: A playful defusion exercise where a client sings a sticky thought to a familiar tune.
goal: Use it to loosen the grip of a sticky thought by changing how it's delivered.
body_md: In session, have the client say a sticky thought out loud in their normal voice, then sing the exact same words to a familiar tune like Happy Birthday, and notice what shifts. Some clients feel silly and rush through it; slow them down and ask what changed about the thought's weight, not just whether it was funny. This works best as an in-session demonstration before asking a client to try it on their own between sessions.

fields.label: Say the sticky thought out loud, in your normal voice.
Now sing the same words to a tune you know well.
What changed about how the thought felt?
Did the thought's content change, or just how it landed?
When this week could you try this with a thought that shows up?

title: Values Implementation Intentions Sheet
summary: A worksheet that turns a value into a specific if-then plan for the coming week.
goal: Use it to close the gap between naming a value and actually acting on it.
body_md: The client picks one value and writes a specific if-then plan: when a named situation comes up this week, they will take a named action in line with that value. Clients often write the value side clearly but leave the action vague, such as be more present; push for something observable enough that another person could see them do it. Review the plan next session and troubleshoot whichever part, the trigger or the action, didn't hold up.

fields.label: Which value do you want to bring into this week?
What situation is likely to come up where this value matters?
Finish this: If [situation], then I will [specific action].
What might get in the way of following through?
How will you know, afterward, that you did it?

title: Raisin Mindfulness Exercise
summary: A slow, sense-by-sense exercise of noticing a small piece of food before eating it.
goal: Use it to give a client a first, concrete taste of present-moment noticing.
body_md: Hand the client a raisin or another small piece of food and walk them through noticing its look, texture, and smell before slowly eating it, pausing at each step. Clients often eat quickly out of habit before the exercise gets going, so name that upfront as the very thing you're practicing noticing. Debrief by asking what they noticed that they wouldn't have on a normal day, and connect that to bringing the same noticing to a daily routine of their choosing.

fields.label: Before eating, describe how it looks and feels in your hand.
What do you notice about its smell?
Eat it slowly. What do you notice about the first taste?
Did you catch yourself wanting to rush? When?
What's one daily moment you could bring this same noticing to?

title: ACT Matrix Worksheet
summary: A four-quadrant diagram sorting a client's inner experience from their toward and away moves.
goal: Use it to map the difference between moving toward values and moving away from discomfort.
body_md: Draw the two crossing lines of the matrix with the client: one axis for what shows up inside versus what shows up in the world, the other for moves away from discomfort versus moves toward what matters. Sort recent behaviors into the four quadrants together, and expect early confusion between toward and away moves that look similar from the outside but feel different on the inside. The finished matrix becomes a quick check-in tool for later sessions.

fields.label: What thoughts, feelings or sensations show up that you'd rather not have?
What do you do to get away from those, in the moment?
Who and what matters to you, even when it's hard?
What would you do more of if you were moving toward that?
Looking at your four quadrants, which move shows up most often?

title: Safe Distance Observer Practice
summary: Helps a client step back and watch triggered thoughts and body sensations from a safe distance.
goal: Use it to build a felt sense of distance from triggered thoughts and sensations.
body_md: Guide the client to notice a triggered thought or sensation, then imagine watching it from a step back, as if seated in a different chair, while both feet stay planted on the floor. People often try to push the sensation away instead of just watching it; gently redirect back to noticing without judging. Stop and ground with breath or feet-on-floor contact if activation climbs, and never use this to explore or narrate what happened, only what is happening in the room right now.

fields.label: What thought or sensation showed up just now?
If you took a step back and just watched it, what do you notice?
What do your feet feel like on the floor right now?
On a scale of 1 to 10, how activated do you feel right now?
What is one thing in this room you can see, right now?

title: Acting Alongside the Fog Practice
summary: Guides a client to take one values-based step while low mood is still present.
goal: Use it to practice moving with depression's fog instead of waiting for it to clear.
body_md: Ask the client to name a mental fog or heaviness that shows up with low mood, then pick one small values-aligned action to take alongside it rather than after it lifts. Clients often make waiting for the fog to clear a precondition for acting; use this practice to separate the feeling from the doing. Keep the chosen action genuinely small, and afterward ask what changed and what stayed exactly the same, since the fog not lifting is an expected, workable outcome here, not a failure of the exercise.

fields.label: Describe the fog or heaviness in your own words.
Name one small action that matters to you, regardless of the fog.
What did you do, alongside the fog, today?
What changed after you acted? What stayed the same?
Was waiting for the fog to lift part of your plan? What if it wasn't required?

title: Boredom Willingness Practice for Tasks
summary: Builds willingness to sit with boredom during a low-stimulation task.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for boredom without needing to escape the task.
body_md: Have the client pick one genuinely boring but necessary task and practice noticing the urge to escape it as a physical sensation rather than acting on it right away, timing how long they can stay willing to feel bored before taking a planned break. Clients often frame boredom as unbearable rather than uncomfortable; help them separate the two. Keep the timed stretch short enough to succeed, then gradually extend it session over session, treating each willing minute as the actual goal rather than how much of the task got finished.

fields.label: What task are you practicing with today?
Where do you feel the urge to escape boredom in your body?
How many minutes were you willing to stay with it?
What did you do instead of acting on the urge to switch?
What would a slightly longer stretch look like next time?

title: Anger Messenger Defusion Practice
summary: Frames an angry thought as a messenger to notice, not an order to follow.
goal: Use it to create space between an angry thought and the action it's pushing for.
body_md: When an angry thought shows up, have the client say it in the form 'my mind is delivering the message that...' and then ask what the message wants them to do right now. Clients often fuse the message with a command they must obey immediately; practice noticing the gap between hearing the message and choosing the action. Once there's space, check the wanted action against what actually matters to the client in that relationship or moment, and pick from there rather than from the message alone.

fields.label: What is the angry thought, word for word?
Say it as 'my mind is delivering the message that...' What message is it?
What action is the message pushing you toward?
What actually matters to you in this moment or relationship?
What will you choose to do, having heard the message?

title: Doubt Surfing Practice
summary: Guides someone to ride out a wave of doubt instead of resolving it.
goal: Use it to build tolerance for doubt without checking, asking, or reviewing.
body_md: Modeled on urge surfing, this has the client notice the pull to seek certainty, rate how strong it feels, and simply watch it rise and fall without acting on it; most people expect the pull to keep climbing forever, so the surprise is usually how much it drops within a few minutes once no ritual follows it.

fields.label: What is the doubt telling me I need to check or confirm?
Rate the pull to resolve it right now, zero to ten.
Where do I feel it in my body?
What happens to the pull after a few minutes if I don't act on it?
What did I do instead of chasing certainty?

title: Panic Committed Action Bridge
summary: Plans one values-based action to take even while fearing another panic attack.
goal: Use it to keep life moving forward between panic episodes, not around them.
body_md: Use this after the acute fear has settled, not during an episode, to identify an activity the client has been avoiding, connect it to something that matters to them, and break it into a step small enough to actually attempt this week; watch for a step chosen so small it never really tests the avoidance.

fields.label: What have I been putting off because I'm afraid of having another panic attack?
What does doing this connect to that matters to me?
What is one step small enough to try this week?
What will I do if a panic attack starts while I'm doing it?

title: Holding Both Selves Practice
summary: Helps a new parent hold their old identity and new role side by side.
goal: Use it to loosen the either/or pull between who someone was and who they are now.
body_md: Have the client list parts of their pre-baby self they miss alongside parts of new-parent life they are starting to value, then practice language of both rather than framing it as who they used to be versus who they are now; resist reassuring them their old self is still fully intact, and watch for this sliding into grief work that needs more room than one exercise allows.

fields.label: Something about who I was before that I still value.
Something about being a parent that I'm starting to value.
Can both of these be true about me right now?
What is one small way to make room for the old self this week?

title: Achievements Aside Self Practice
summary: Separates a sense of worth from the day's list of wins and failures.
goal: Use it to practice a sense of self that doesn't rise and fall with performance.
body_md: Have the client set today's wins and failures aside on paper and notice what, if anything, remains true about them either way; this is a self-as-context exercise rather than a pep talk, so resist reassuring the client their achievements are actually good, and watch for it being used to dismiss real accomplishments instead of decoupling worth from them.

fields.label: List today's wins and today's failures.
Set the list aside. What is still true about me either way?
What does it feel like to imagine worth that isn't earned or lost?
What is one moment today I can practice this?

title: Should Be Over It by Now Defusion Practice
summary: Defuses from judgmental thoughts about how a client 'should' be grieving.
goal: Use it to loosen the grip of timeline judgments a client makes about their own grief.
body_md: Use this when a client criticizes themselves for still grieving, comparing their pace to some imagined timeline. Have them say the judgmental thought aloud, then add the defusion frame ('I'm having the thought that I should be over this by now') and notice what shifts in how much the thought pulls at them. Some clients resist the exercise because it can feel like permission to stay stuck; clarify that defusion loosens the thought's grip, it does not endorse or argue with it. Watch for a client who intellectualizes the practice instead of actually trying it out loud.

fields.label: The judgmental thought about my grief timeline, in my own words…
Now with 'I'm having the thought that...' in front of it…
What I notice in my body saying it that way…
How much this thought pulled at me before, 0 to 10…
How much it pulls at me now, 0 to 10…

title: Needing to Win Defusion Practice
summary: Defuses from the urge to win an argument instead of staying connected.
goal: Use it to help a client notice the pull to be right and choose a value-driven response instead.
body_md: Bring this out after a client describes an argument they 'won' but that left the relationship worse off. Have them name the thought driving the fight ('I have to make them admit I'm right'), then practice noticing it as a thought passing through rather than a command to obey, and ask what mattered more in that moment — winning or staying connected. Clients who pride themselves on debate skill may resist this, framing defusion as giving up ground; reframe it as choosing which fight is worth having. Watch for the exercise turning into another way to feel superior to the partner.

fields.label: The argument where I really wanted to win…
The thought that was driving me to win…
Saying 'I'm noticing the thought that I need to win this'…
What I actually wanted from this argument underneath winning…
What I'd choose to do next time this thought shows up…

title: Observing Self Safety Practice
summary: Uses an observing-self stance to notice body alarm signals from a safe distance.
goal: Use it to help a client notice body signals in the present without being swept into them.
body_md: Run this in session when a client's body reacts strongly to something in the here and now — a sound, a posture, a smell — and they feel pulled into the sensation rather than simply having it. Guide them to notice the sensation from the stance of an observer watching it happen, naming it without narrating any past event: what the body is doing right now, in this room, today. This stays entirely present-focused, never a place to describe what happened. If a client starts recounting past details, gently redirect back to present sensations and the safety of the current room.

fields.label: The sensation I'm noticing in my body right now…
Where in my body I notice it most…
From the observer part of me, what I see this sensation doing…
One thing in this room right now that tells me I'm safe…
How the sensation is different now than when we started…

title: Can't Handle It Defusion Practice
summary: Defuses from the thought that a client can't handle being near a feared object.
goal: Use it to loosen a client's belief that fear itself is proof they can't cope.
body_md: Use this right before or during an approach step when a client says something like 'I can't handle this' as their fear rises. Have them notice the thought, add the defusion frame ('I'm having the thought that I can't handle this'), then check what's actually happening in their body and the room right now, separate from the thought's prediction. This isn't about proving the thought wrong through argument; it's about taking a step with the thought present rather than waiting for it to vanish first. Watch for a client who uses defusion as a stalling tactic instead of continuing the step.

fields.label: The situation where this thought shows up…
The thought in its original form…
The thought with 'I'm having the thought that...' added…
What's actually true in this room right now, separate from the thought…
What I can do next with the thought still present…

title: Checking Urge Surf and Defuse Practice
summary: Rides out the urge to mirror-check or compare instead of acting on it right away.
goal: Use it to help a client notice a checking urge pass without acting on it every time.
body_md: Use this when a client notices the pull to check a mirror, photo, or reflection repeatedly through the day. Have them pause when the urge hits, name it out loud as an urge rather than a need, and time how long it takes to ease off while doing something else. Most urges peak and fall within a few minutes if not acted on, and clients rarely expect that. Watch for a client who checks once as an experiment and calls the practice a failure — the goal is noticing the urge pass, not eliminating checking overnight.

fields.label: Where I am and what triggered the urge to check…
Rating the urge to check, 0 to 10, right when it starts…
What I did instead of checking…
The urge rating after a few minutes…
What I noticed about how the urge changed…

title: Cheerleading Statements Card
summary: A pocket card of self-encouraging statements a client rehearses before a hard moment.
goal: Use it to replace a client's harsh self-talk with statements they can actually believe.
body_md: The client writes several short, believable self-encouraging statements, such as I can do this one step at a time rather than an empty everything is fine, and picks the situations where they'll use them. Clients often reach for statements that are too rosy to trust in the moment, which backfires; steer them toward something true enough to hold up under stress. Have them read the card out loud in session and notice which lines land and which still feel hollow.

fields.label: Write three statements you could actually believe when things get hard.
Which one feels most believable right now?
What situation this week could you use this card in?
Read each statement out loud. Which one feels hollow?
Rewrite any that feel hollow into something truer.

title: One-Mindfully Focus Practice
summary: A short practice of doing exactly one thing at a time and noticing the pull to multitask.
goal: Use it to build a client's capacity to stay with one task without splitting attention.
body_md: Pick one everyday task with the client, washing a dish or walking to the mailbox, and have them do only that, bringing attention back each time it drifts to something else. Clients usually notice the pull to multitask within seconds and treat it as failure; reframe each return of attention as the actual practice, not a sign it isn't working. Build up from one task a day to a few, and log what pulled attention away most often.

fields.label: What one task will you do one-mindfully today?
How many times did your attention drift during the task?
What pulled your attention away?
What did you notice about the task itself when you stayed with it?
What task will you try this with tomorrow?

title: Acceptance and Change Goal Planner
summary: A goal sheet that pairs each goal with one thing to accept alongside it.
goal: Use it to help a client hold acceptance and change side by side instead of choosing one.
body_md: For each goal the client sets, they also name one part of the current situation they need to accept as true right now in order to work toward it without being derailed by wishing things were already different. Clients often resist the acceptance side, treating it as giving up; clarify that accepting what's currently true is what frees up energy for the change itself. Revisit both columns together at each check-in.

fields.label: What's one goal you want to work toward?
What's currently true that you'd need to accept to work toward it calmly?
What's one small step toward the goal this week?
What tends to happen when you fight the thing you need to accept?
How will accepting it change what you do differently?
