title: Mindful Pause Bell Practice
summary: A practice of pausing whenever a bell or cue sounds to notice the present moment.
goal: Use it to build a habit of brief mindful pauses scattered through an ordinary day.
duration: Five minutes daily for several weeks
body_md: The client picks a recurring cue already in their day, a phone alarm, a red light, a kettle, and pauses for three slow breaths and a quick body scan whenever it happens, logging what they noticed. The most common trip-up is picking a cue that's too rare to build the habit, or forgetting the log entirely; a cue that happens several times a day works best. Use the log to spot which times of day the client is most scattered.

fields.label: What cue will you use to trigger your pause?
Each time it happens, what did you notice in your body?
What were you doing right before the cue went off?
How many pauses did you catch today?
What time of day were you hardest to pause?

title: Alternate Rebellion Idea Bank
summary: A list of small, harmless rule-breaks a client can use instead of a riskier one.
goal: Use it to give a client a safer outlet for the urge to break a rule or push back.
body_md: The client brainstorms small, harmless ways to scratch the itch of rebelling, wearing mismatched socks, taking a different route home, staying up late reading, to have on hand when the urge to break a bigger rule shows up. Clients sometimes can't tell the difference between an urge to rebel and an urge tied to something else entirely, like anger or boredom; help them sort the list by what the urge is actually about. Keep the bank updated as old ideas lose their charge.

fields.label: What rule or expectation do you feel the urge to push back against?
List five small, harmless ways you could rebel instead.
Which one could you use the next time the urge shows up?
What is the urge actually about underneath the rebellion?
How did it go the last time you tried one of these?

title: Wise Mind Anchor Phrase Card
summary: Gives a client a short wise mind phrase to repeat when a trauma reminder spikes arousal.
goal: Use it to build a fast, portable anchor for moments of high activation.
body_md: In session, help the client craft one short phrase that names the present moment as safe enough right now, such as 'that was then, this is now, I am here.' Write it on a card they can keep in a pocket or phone. People often reach for a long explanation instead of a short phrase; keep it to one breath's worth of words. Practice saying it out loud together while the client notices their feet or hands, and check that the wording feels true rather than forced before they leave with it.

fields.label: Write your anchor phrase in your own words.
Where will you keep this card so it's easy to find?
What does your body feel like as you say the phrase slowly?
Who is one person you could say this phrase out loud with?
What situation this week might call for this card?

title: Low-Mood Prediction Fact-Check Card
summary: Checks a depressive prediction against the actual facts of a specific situation.
goal: Use it to slow down a low-mood prediction long enough to check it against facts.
body_md: Have the client name a specific prediction low mood is making about an upcoming situation, like 'it will be pointless,' then walk through the actual facts available right now rather than the felt certainty. This is a direct application of checking the facts, aimed specifically at the flat, foregone-conclusion quality low mood gives predictions. Clients often say the facts don't matter because the feeling is so strong; note that down as data rather than arguing with it, and revisit the card after the situation actually happens.

fields.label: What is low mood predicting about this situation?
What are the actual facts you know right now?
How certain does the prediction feel, 0 to 100?
What happened afterward, compared to the prediction?
What will you check the facts on next?

title: Opposite Action for Task Avoidance Card
summary: Applies opposite action to the urge to avoid a boring or overwhelming task.
goal: Use it to practice starting a task despite the urge to put it off.
body_md: When the client notices the urge to avoid a task, have them name the urge and its opposite action, such as opening the document instead of closing the tab, then commit to two minutes of the opposite action only. This is opposite action applied specifically to task avoidance rather than to an emotion, so keep the ask small and time-boxed. Clients often wait for motivation before starting; note that the opposite action is meant to come before any change in how they feel, not after it.

fields.label: What task are you avoiding right now?
What is the urge telling you to do instead?
What is the opposite action, in one small step?
Did you do two minutes of the opposite action? What happened?
What made starting easier or harder than expected?

title: Life Worth Living Recovery Card
summary: Names concrete pieces of a life worth living to weigh against substance use urges.
goal: Use it to keep a concrete, positive reason for change in view during hard moments.
body_md: Ask the client to name a few specific, believable pieces of a life they want to build, not abstractions, and write them on a card small enough to carry. When an urge shows up, the card is a quick way to check the moment against the bigger picture rather than arguing with the urge directly. Clients sometimes reach for a vague or idealized version of their life; keep pushing for specifics they actually recognize as theirs. Update the card together every few sessions as what matters to them shifts.

fields.label: Name three specific things that would be part of a life worth living for you.
Which one feels most within reach right now?
When an urge shows up, what would using take away from this list?
What is one action this week that moves toward this list?
What would you add or change on this card today?

title: Radically Accepting Uncertainty Log
summary: Applies radical acceptance to the not-knowing that intrusive thoughts demand answers for.
goal: Use it to practice accepting uncertainty rather than fighting for proof.
body_md: Run the client through the radical acceptance steps applied specifically to a moment of not-knowing rather than to suffering in general; clarify carefully that accepting the uncertainty is not the same as accepting that the feared outcome is true, since that fusion is where this exercise most often goes sideways for someone with intrusive thoughts.

fields.label: What am I being asked to accept not knowing for certain?
What does my body do when I stop trying to resolve it?
What would radically accepting this moment look like?
What is one small way I can practice that today?

title: Cold Water Reset Card
summary: Uses a fast temperature change to bring a racing panic response down quickly.
goal: Use it to teach the temperature half of TIPP as a quick physical reset.
body_md: Practice this in session first, holding cold water on the face or wrists or gripping ice, and check for any heart condition before recommending it as homework; hand over the card once the client has felt the reset happen once with you, and watch for it becoming a way to avoid ever letting a milder wave of panic simply pass on its own.

fields.label: Where can I keep something cold within reach, like the fridge or a bathroom sink?
How did my body feel right before I used it?
How did it feel about thirty seconds after?
When would I reach for this versus just riding the wave out?

title: Opposite Action for Postpartum Withdrawal
summary: Uses opposite action to counter the pull to hide from support when things feel hard.
goal: Use it to practice reaching out even when shame urges someone to withdraw.
body_md: Walk through the standard opposite action steps applied to withdrawing from a partner or friends: name the emotion driving the pull, often shame or overwhelm, check whether hiding actually fits the facts of the situation, then plan a small opposite action such as one short text or accepting a single offer of help; watch for the action being done so partially it never actually creates contact.

fields.label: What emotion is pulling me to withdraw right now?
Does hiding actually fit the facts of the situation?
What would the opposite action look like, specifically?
Who is one person I could reach out to today?

title: Opposite Action for Self-Doubt
summary: Uses opposite action to counter the urge to shrink back when self-worth feels shaky.
goal: Use it to practice showing up despite the pull to hide or downplay oneself.
body_md: Walk through opposite action steps applied to the urge to stay quiet, avoid eye contact, or minimize oneself when self-doubt spikes; check whether the urge fits the facts of the moment, then plan one small opposite action such as speaking up once in a meeting or accepting a compliment out loud, and watch for a client choosing an action so small it doesn't register as a real stretch.

fields.label: What is the urge to shrink back telling me to do right now?
Does that urge actually fit the facts of the situation?
What would the opposite action look like, specifically?
What happened in my body when I tried it?

title: GIVE Skills for Small Talk
summary: Applies the GIVE skill to the specific discomfort of making small talk.
goal: Use it to give someone a concrete script for GIVE in low-stakes conversation.
body_md: Walk through each letter of gentle, interested, validate, and easy manner with a small-talk example, then have the client script one actual line for each before their next low-stakes conversation; watch for over-scripting to the point that the exchange feels rehearsed rather than easier, since the goal is a starting point, not a transcript to memorize.

fields.label: Gentle: one thing I could say without an edge to it.
Interested: one question I could ask the other person.
Validate: one thing I could say back that shows I heard them.
Easy manner: one small bit of humor or lightness I could add.
Which of these feels hardest to actually do?

title: Radical Acceptance of Partner Differences Practice
summary: Applies radical acceptance to a partner trait a client keeps fighting.
goal: Use it to help a client stop the extra suffering of refusing to accept a fixed difference.
body_md: Use this for a client stuck resenting a partner trait unlikely to change — a difference in tidiness, sociability, or emotional expression — rather than an active safety concern. Walk through radical acceptance: naming the difference as real, noticing the added suffering the resistance itself creates, and practicing a phrase that accepts the fact without approving of it. Clients sometimes confuse acceptance with agreeing the difference is fine; clarify it means dropping the fight against reality while still deciding what boundaries or requests make sense.

fields.label: The difference between us I keep fighting against…
How I usually react when this difference shows up…
What refusing to accept this costs me…
A radical acceptance phrase I can say to myself…
What I can still ask for or set a boundary about, separate from acceptance…

title: TIPP for Body Alarm Spikes Card
summary: Walks a client through TIPP skills when body alarm spikes in session.
goal: Use it to bring a client's intense physical distress down fast and safely in session.
body_md: Keep this card ready for a moment in session when a client's distress spikes hard and fast — racing heart, shaking, feeling unable to stay in the room. Walk them through one TIPP option live: cold water on the face or hands, paced exhale-longer breathing, or brief intense movement, whatever fits your space. This is a here-and-now tool done together in session, not homework for a crisis alone; if distress is severe or the client mentions wanting to end their life, name 988 (call or text) as an option right then. Watch for a client who uses it to suppress the spike rather than ride it out.

fields.label: What I'm noticing in my body right now, from head to toe…
The TIPP option I'm trying right now: cold, paced breathing, or movement…
My distress level before, 0 to 10…
My distress level after a few minutes…
If this gets worse when I'm not with my therapist, 988 (call or text) is here…

title: Opposite Action Approach Card
summary: Uses opposite action to move toward a feared object instead of away from it.
goal: Use it to help a client act against the urge to avoid when fear doesn't fit the actual risk.
body_md: Use this with a client who agrees the fear they feel around a specific object or situation is out of proportion to the actual risk. Walk through the opposite action steps: name the fear, check whether it fits the facts, and if it doesn't, commit to acting opposite to the avoidance urge all the way — approaching fully rather than halfway. Half-hearted opposite action tends to backfire, so coach the client toward a step they can complete fully rather than a bigger one they'll bail out of partway through.

fields.label: The fear and the situation it shows up in…
Does the fear fit the actual risk here? Why or why not…
The avoidance urge I'm noticing…
The opposite action I'll take, all the way through…
How it went, and what I noticed in my body afterward…

title: Opposite Action for Appearance Avoidance Card
summary: Uses opposite action to face situations a client avoids due to appearance shame.
goal: Use it to help a client re-enter situations they skip because of how they think they look.
body_md: Use this with a client who skips photos, gatherings, or activities specifically because of shame about their appearance. Check whether the shame fits the actual situation — is anyone actually going to judge them the way they fear — and if it doesn't fit, walk through committing to the opposite action of showing up fully rather than partially. A client might attend but hide at the edges, which blunts the exercise; coach toward full participation for it to work. Note what the client notices afterward about how much attention others actually paid to their appearance.

fields.label: The situation I usually avoid because of how I think I look…
The shame I feel about it…
Does that shame fit what's actually likely to happen? Why or why not…
The opposite action I'll commit to, fully…
What I noticed afterward, especially about others' attention…

title: Shared Vision Conversation Cards
summary: A set of conversation prompts where partners describe the life they picture together.
goal: Use it to help partners compare their long-term pictures before setting shared goals.
body_md: Partner A and Partner B each answer the same set of prompts about where they picture themselves in five or ten years, separately at first, then read their answers to each other. Couples often assume they already know each other's picture and are surprised by a gap in timing or priority; treat any mismatch as information to plan around, not a problem to resolve on the spot. Use the overlaps to draft one or two shared goals to revisit later.

fields.label: Partner A: describe a normal day in your life five years from now.
Partner B: describe a normal day in your life five years from now.
Where do your two pictures overlap?
Where do they pull in different directions?
What's one shared goal you could set based on the overlap?

title: Personal Space Needs Negotiation
summary: A worksheet where each partner names how much separate time and space they need.
goal: Use it to turn a vague tension over togetherness into a concrete, workable agreement.
body_md: Partner A and Partner B each estimate how much time alone or with separate friends they need in a typical week, then compare numbers and negotiate a plan both can live with. The conversation often stalls when one partner hears the other's need for space as rejection; name that reading out loud and separate the need from what it means about the relationship. Write the agreed plan down and revisit it if either partner's needs shift.

fields.label: Partner A: how much time alone do you need most weeks?
Partner B: how much time alone do you need most weeks?
What does it feel like when your partner asks for space?
Where do your numbers create tension?
What plan can you both agree to try this month?

title: Shared Decision Values Grid
summary: A grid where partners score a shared decision against each of their own values.
goal: Use it to help a couple see where their values agree and where they diverge on a choice.
body_md: Partner A and Partner B each list what matters to them about a decision they're facing together, then score the options on the table against both lists side by side. Couples often discover they've been arguing about the decision itself when the real gap is in which value should win when two matter at once; slow down and name that trade-off directly. Use the grid to negotiate which value takes priority this time, and note it for next time.

fields.label: What decision are you facing together?
Partner A: what matters most to you about it?
Partner B: what matters most to you about it?
Where do your value lists agree?
Where do they pull in different directions, and how will you decide?

title: Talking Stick Turn-Taking Exercise
summary: A structured exercise where only the partner holding an object may speak.
goal: Use it to slow down a conversation so each partner is fully heard before replying.
body_md: Give the couple any small object to pass back and forth: only the partner holding it may speak, and the other must reflect back what they heard before asking for the object themselves. Partners usually break the rule within the first minute by jumping in to correct or defend; gently reset the object rather than letting the conversation slide back into normal cross-talk. Run it on a low-stakes topic first before using it for a harder conversation.

fields.label: Partner A: while holding the object, share your view without interruption.
Partner B: reflect back what you heard before responding.
Partner B: now share your view, holding the object.
Partner A: reflect back what you heard.
What was different about being heard this way?

title: Shared Daily Routine Redesign
summary: A worksheet where partners map their daily routines and redesign the friction points.
goal: Use it to help a couple rebuild shared routines that have quietly stopped working.
body_md: Partner A and Partner B each sketch out a typical weekday hour by hour, then compare charts to find moments where their routines collide, conflict, or leave one partner carrying more than the other. Couples often find the friction point is a small logistics issue rather than a bigger relationship problem; resist the urge to over-interpret a scheduling clash. Pick one friction point to redesign together and try the new routine for a week before reviewing.

fields.label: Partner A: sketch your typical weekday, hour by hour.
Partner B: sketch your typical weekday, hour by hour.
Where do your two routines collide or create friction?
Which one friction point will you redesign first?
What will you try instead this week?

title: Nightmare Aftermath Support Plan
summary: Plans how each partner responds when one wakes from a trauma-related nightmare.
goal: Use it to turn a startled overnight moment into a rehearsed, calmer routine for both partners.
body_md: Have each partner describe, separately then together, what actually helps them return to feeling safe after a nightmare and what unintentionally makes it worse, such as being touched suddenly or being asked what the dream was about. Couples often default to the waking partner's own instincts rather than what their partner has said helps; slow this down and write both preferences on the same page. The tool never asks either partner to recount the dream content itself, only what helps them settle afterward, and works best rehearsed calmly rather than introduced for the first time overnight.

fields.label: Partner having the nightmare: what usually helps you feel safe again?
Partner having the nightmare: what should your partner NOT do in that moment?
Supporting partner: what do you tend to do right now when this happens?
Both: what will your partner say or do first, before anything else?
Both: how will you check in with each other the next morning?

title: Worry Spillover Conversation for Partners
summary: Helps both partners name how one partner's worry affects the other and set limits.
goal: Use it to separate supporting a worried partner from absorbing their worry.
body_md: Have the worried partner describe what kind of support actually helps versus what just moves the worry onto their partner, such as needing repeated reassurance late in the evening. Have the other partner name where they feel the spillover in their own mood or sleep, without blame. Couples often skip straight to 'stop worrying' as the ask; redirect toward a specific, workable limit both partners can agree to, like a set reassurance window each evening. Revisit the agreement after a week rather than expecting it to hold perfectly the first time.

fields.label: Worried partner: what kind of support actually helps you in the moment?
Worried partner: what does your partner do that doesn't help, even if well meant?
Other partner: where do you notice the worry landing on you?
Both: what is one specific limit you can agree to try this week?
Both: when will you check back in on how the limit is working?

title: Interruption Pattern Repair Conversation
summary: Helps both partners name and repair a pattern of interrupting during talks.
goal: Use it to turn a recurring interruption pattern into a repairable, non-blaming routine.
body_md: Have the interrupting partner describe what pulls their attention mid-conversation and how it feels from the inside, while the other partner describes what it feels like to be cut off, without either side turning it into a character judgment. Couples often land on 'you don't care' or 'you can't help it' as the whole story; push past both to a workable repair signal, like a hand gesture that means 'let me finish,' that either partner can use in the moment. Practice the signal once in session before sending it home as homework.

fields.label: Interrupting partner: what usually pulls your attention away mid-sentence?
Other partner: what does it feel like when this happens?
What signal will you use to mean 'let me finish'?
What will the interrupting partner do when they see that signal?
How will you check in with each other after trying this for a week?

title: Recovery Trust Milestones Conversation
summary: Names concrete trust milestones both partners can track as recovery continues.
goal: Use it to give both partners a shared, specific way to track rebuilding trust.
body_md: Have both partners name specific, observable milestones that would signal trust is rebuilding, such as an agreed check-in call or an unprompted update, rather than a vague sense of 'feeling better about it.' The partner in recovery names what support would actually help hit each milestone, and the other partner names what checking in without becoming a monitor could look like. Couples often set either impossibly high or vague milestones; keep pushing both toward something specific and time-bound, and revisit the list together every few weeks.

fields.label: Partner in recovery: what is one specific milestone that would show progress?
Partner in recovery: what support would help you reach it?
Other partner: what would checking in, without monitoring, look like for you?
Both: what milestone will you track over the next two weeks?
Both: how will you know, together, that it's been met?

title: Ritual Participation Boundary Script
summary: Helps both partners agree on which rituals the partner will stop taking part in.
goal: Use it to script a caring way to step back from performing rituals together.
body_md: Have each partner name the specific tasks the supporting partner currently does or repeats, such as double-checking locks or answering the same question, agree on one to phase out first, and script a short caring line to say instead of doing it; expect pushback or guilt in the first attempts and plan for it rather than treating a single setback as failure.

fields.label: Partner A: which rituals do I currently take part in or complete for you?
Partner B: which of these would you like help stepping back from first?
What can Partner A say instead of doing the ritual?
How will we handle it if things feel harder at first?
How will we notice and mark progress together?

title: Supporter Burnout Check-In
summary: Gives the partner who does the reassuring a space to name their own strain.
goal: Use it to check the supporting partner isn't quietly wearing thin.
body_md: Unlike tools about what to do during or after an episode, this one centers what repeated support has cost the supporting partner; have them name the hardest part and what they need for themselves, and have the partner with panic simply listen without jumping to reassure them back or apologize the conversation away.

fields.label: Partner supporting: what has been hardest about being the calm one during these episodes?
Partner supporting: what do you need more of for yourself?
Partner with panic: what did you not know about the cost to your partner?
What is one thing we can change so support is sustainable?

title: Parenting Style Differences Map
summary: Names both partners' upbringing-shaped instincts before they clash over a child.
goal: Use it to trace parenting reactions back to each partner's own upbringing.
body_md: Have each partner recall how their own parents typically handled one recurring flashpoint, such as bedtime or tantrums, then compare where their instincts agree and where they pull apart, ending with one shared approach to try for that specific moment; keep the conversation on today's approach rather than letting it turn into re-litigating either partner's childhood.

fields.label: Partner A: how did your own parents typically handle this kind of moment?
Partner B: how did your own parents typically handle this kind of moment?
Where do our instincts agree?
Where do they pull in different directions?
What is one shared approach we can try this week?

title: Low Self-Worth Support Signal
summary: Gives both partners a private signal for when self-worth dips need support.
goal: Use it to agree on how one partner can ask for support without over-explaining.
body_md: Have the partner who struggles with self-worth name the situations that tend to trigger a dip and agree on a low-effort signal, a word or gesture, that tells their partner support is wanted; the supporting partner names what they usually do that lands as fixing or over-reassuring instead of helping, and both agree on one thing to try next time the signal appears.

fields.label: Partner with the dip: what situations tend to trigger it?
Partner with the dip: what signal could tell your partner you need support?
Supporting partner: what do you usually do that doesn't quite land?
Supporting partner: what will you try instead when you see the signal?

title: Social Event Wingman Plan
summary: Names how a partner can help without hovering at a social event.
goal: Use it to agree on specific support at events, not blanket rescuing.
body_md: Have the anxious partner name what actually helps at an event, such as an exit signal, a check-in every twenty minutes, or being introduced rather than left to start conversations alone, versus what feels like being babysat; the supporting partner names what they need in return, like permission to also enjoy the event, and watch for a plan that leaves the anxious partner never having to initiate anything.

fields.label: Partner with anxiety: what kind of support actually helps at an event?
Partner with anxiety: what feels like being babysat instead of supported?
Supporting partner: what do you need so this doesn't fall only on you?
What is our signal if it's time to leave or take a break?

title: Speaker-Listener Turn Card
summary: Structures a hard conversation into speaker and listener turns with a hand-off object.
goal: Use it to slow a couple's conversation enough for each partner to actually be heard.
body_md: Give the couple a small object to pass between them — only the partner holding it may speak, in short statements, while the other partner listens and then paraphrases before responding. Switch the object after each paraphrase is accepted as accurate. Couples used to interrupting each other find the pacing awkward at first and may want to abandon it mid-conversation; encourage them to finish one full round before deciding it isn't working. Watch for a listening partner who paraphrases the words but not the feeling underneath them.

fields.label: Partner A: what I want to say, in one or two short sentences…
Partner B: what I heard Partner A say…
Partner A: did that paraphrase land? What's still missing…
Partner B: what I want to say now that it's my turn…
Partner A: what I heard Partner B say…
Both: what felt different about talking this way…

title: Pause Signal Agreement for Partners
summary: Sets a shared signal both partners use to pause touch in the moment.
goal: Use it to give both partners a clear, low-pressure way to pause physical closeness.
body_md: Have both partners agree on a simple word or gesture either one can use, at any point, to pause physical touch without needing to explain why in the moment. Practice it once in session on something low-stakes, like a hand-hold, so both partners feel what a respected pause looks like. The partner receiving the signal responds only with acknowledgment, saving questions or hurt feelings for a later conversation. This stays on present-moment pacing and consent, never on reviewing past events; if either partner starts describing a past incident in detail, redirect to the agreement itself.

fields.label: Partner A: the word or gesture I'll use to signal pause…
Partner B: how I'll respond when I see or hear that signal…
Partner A: what I need after a pause before we continue…
Partner B: what I need to hear to feel okay about a pause…
Both: when we'll check in about how the signal is working…

title: Partner Coping Support Handoff Plan
summary: Plans what each partner does when the other reaches for a coping skill mid-stress.
goal: Use it to help partners support each other's coping without taking it over.
body_md: Have each partner separately name their own two or three go-to coping skills, then swap sheets and talk through what the other partner can do to make room for that skill — stepping back, staying nearby without talking, or offering a specific phrase. This heads off a common pattern where a supportive partner accidentally interrupts coping by hovering or asking too many questions in the moment. Have both partners agree on one small cue the coping partner can give — a word or gesture — that means 'give me a few minutes,' and check back in a few weeks on whether the handoff is working.

fields.label: Partner A: my go-to coping skills are…
Partner A: what helps me use them, and what gets in the way…
Partner B: what I'll do to make room for Partner A's coping skill…
Partner B: my go-to coping skills are…
Partner A: what I'll do to make room for Partner B's coping skill…
Both: our cue for 'give me a few minutes' is…

title: Appearance Comment Ground Rules for Partners
summary: Sets shared rules for how partners talk about each other's appearance.
goal: Use it to help partners agree on what appearance comments help versus hurt.
body_md: Have each partner separately list appearance-related comments that help them and ones that land badly, even when well-intended, then compare lists together. A common surprise is a comment meant as reassurance landing as pressure to look a certain way; naming this out loud heads off repeated missteps. Agree on one or two ground rules going forward, such as complimenting something other than appearance or asking before commenting at all. Revisit the rules if either partner's preferences shift.

fields.label: Partner A: an appearance comment that actually helps me…
Partner A: an appearance comment that lands badly, even if well-meant…
Partner B: an appearance comment that actually helps me…
Partner B: an appearance comment that lands badly, even if well-meant…
Both: one ground rule we're agreeing to going forward…

title: Gratitude Garden Growth Chart
summary: A craft where a child adds a paper flower to a growing garden for each thing they're glad about.
goal: Use it to build a daily gratitude habit a child can see growing on the wall.
duration: Five minutes daily for several weeks
body_md: The child decorates a paper flower and writes or draws one thing they're glad about, adding it to a garden poster on the wall each day; the parent sets aside the same few minutes daily and asks the child to point to their favorite flower so far. Some children run out of new ideas after a few days; the parent can prompt with a specific moment from that day rather than asking a general question. Watch for the child starting to notice good moments unprompted as the garden fills in.

fields.label: Draw or write one thing you're glad about today.
Decorate your flower however you like.
Add it to your garden. How many flowers do you have now?
Which flower is your favorite so far, and why?
Tell a grown-up about one flower today.

title: Solve-It Superhero Comic Strip
summary: A comic strip a child draws showing a superhero solving a small everyday problem step by step.
goal: Use it to teach a child a simple problem-solving sequence through a story they draw.
body_md: The child draws a four-box comic strip where a superhero of their own design notices a problem, thinks of a few ideas, picks one, and tries it out, with the parent asking what happens next at each box. Children often jump straight to the solution box and skip generating more than one idea; the parent can pause and ask what else could the hero try before moving on. Keep finished strips to reference the next time the child faces a real problem of their own.

fields.label: Box 1: draw your superhero noticing a problem.
Box 2: draw or list two or three ideas the hero has.
Box 3: draw the hero picking one idea and trying it.
Box 4: draw what happens next.
What real problem of yours could your hero help with?

title: Speak-Up Puppet Script
summary: A puppet a child makes and uses to practice saying an assertive sentence out loud.
goal: Use it to help a child rehearse standing up for themselves in a low-pressure way.
body_md: The child decorates a simple sock or paper-bag puppet, then uses it to practice saying a short assertive line, such as please stop or I want a turn too, while the parent plays the other character and reacts. Children often mumble the line or laugh it off at first; let the puppet carry the boldness so the child doesn't have to, and repeat the line a few times before ending the session. Praise the specific words used, not just the effort.

fields.label: Decorate your puppet. What's its name?
What's something you wish you could say to someone but haven't?
Practice saying it through your puppet's voice.
How did it feel to say it out loud?
When could you try saying it for real?

title: My Big Goal Treasure Map
summary: A treasure map a child draws with stepping stones leading to a goal marked with an X.
goal: Use it to break a child's big goal into small, visible steps they can check off.
body_md: The child draws a map with their goal marked as buried treasure at one end, then adds stepping stones between the start and the X, each one a small step toward the goal; the parent helps name a realistic first stone and checks in on progress weekly. Children often draw a huge jump straight to the treasure with no stones in between; the parent can ask what would need to happen right before that to work backward into smaller steps.

fields.label: What's your treasure? Draw it and write what it is.
Draw the first stepping stone: what's the very first small step?
Add three more stepping stones between the start and the treasure.
Which stone will you try to reach this week?
Color in a stone each time you reach it.

title: Decision Spinner Wheel Craft
summary: A paper spinner a child builds and uses to weigh choices in a made-up scenario.
goal: Use it to give a child a hands-on way to practice thinking through choices and consequences.
body_md: The child builds a simple paper spinner divided into a few choices for a scenario the parent describes, spins to see which choice comes up, and then talks through what might happen next if they actually picked it. The parent's job is to ask and then what a couple of times after each spin rather than telling the child the right answer. Children sometimes want to keep re-spinning until they land on their favorite choice; that's a fine moment to talk about picking versus wishing.

fields.label: Write three or four choices around your spinner.
Spin it. Which choice did you land on?
What might happen next if you really picked that choice?
Would you actually pick that one, or a different one?
Why?

title: Safety Signal Bracelet Craft
summary: A child builds a wearable bracelet where each bead stands for one calming step.
goal: Use it to give a child a wearable, always-available reminder of their calming steps.
body_md: Have the child string four or five beads, each one matched to a step they choose, such as a deep breath, naming a color in the room, or finding a grown-up. Parents help hold the string steady and can wear a matching bracelet themselves as a cue to check in together. Children sometimes want to add a bead for what scared them; keep the beads focused on calming steps only, not on retelling the event, and gently redirect if a story starts. Remind the parent of their duty to report any new disclosure of harm to the appropriate authority rather than handling it alone.

fields.label: Pick a color for each calming step you want to remember.
What will bead number one remind you to do?
Who will you show your bracelet to?
When might you need to look at your bracelet this week?
Grown-up: what will you do when you see your child touch the bracelet?

title: Try-It Spinner Craft for Worries
summary: A child builds a spinner of small brave actions to try one at a time.
goal: Use it to turn facing worries into a playful, low-stakes daily activity.
body_md: Help the child decorate a paper spinner with four or five small, doable actions that nudge against a specific worry, like saying hello first or trying a new food bite. The parent spins it with the child once a day and celebrates the attempt itself rather than how it turns out. Children sometimes want to skip the spin when it lands on something hard; let them spin again once, but not endlessly, so the exercise stays a stretch rather than an escape. Keep the actions small enough that most spins end in a genuine, sharable win.

fields.label: Draw or write four small brave actions on your spinner.
What did the spinner choose for you today?
How did it feel to try it, before and after?
Grown-up: what did you notice your child do well today?
What small brave action do you want to add next?

title: Task Chunks Visual Chart Craft
summary: A child builds a visual chart that breaks one chore into small stickered chunks.
goal: Use it to make a multi-step task visible and completable one chunk at a time.
body_md: Help the child draw or paste four or five small pictures showing the steps of one chore, like cleaning a room, in the order they happen, leaving a spot for a sticker after each step. The parent sets a timer for just the next chunk rather than the whole chore and sits nearby while the child works. Children often want to jump ahead or skip steps; gently bring them back to the current chunk only. Celebrate the sticker, not the perfection of the finished chunk, and rebuild the chart together if a chore keeps stalling at the same step.

fields.label: Draw the steps of your chore in order.
Which chunk are you working on right now?
What sticker will you add when it's done?
How did that chunk go?
Grown-up: which chunk does your child need the most help starting?

title: My Support People Chain Craft
summary: A child builds a paper chain of trusted adults to talk to on hard or confusing days.
goal: Use it to give a child a visible, ready list of safe adults for hard days at home.
body_md: Have the child decorate paper links, one for each trusted adult they name, such as a parent, teacher, or relative, and link them into a chain to hang somewhere they see often. The parent's job is to help the child pick real, available people and to add their own contact information to one link. Keep the focus on who the child can go to, not on describing what is happening at home, and never ask the child to explain a family member's substance use as part of the activity. Follow your own reporting duties if the child discloses anything concerning while building it.

fields.label: Who is one grown-up you trust? Add them to the chain.
What could you say to them if you needed help?
Where will you hang your chain so you can see it?
Which link would you go to first on a hard day?
Grown-up: how will you check in with your child this week?

title: Where Anger Lives Body Map Craft
summary: A child colors where anger shows up in their body and picks a calming spot for each.
goal: Use it to connect a child's body signals of anger to a specific calming action.
body_md: Give the child an outline of a body and have them color or mark where they notice anger, like a hot face or tight fists, then pick one calming action to pair with each spot, such as cool water on hot hands. The parent helps name spots the child might miss and keeps a copy of the finished map somewhere visible. Children sometimes color the whole body at once when upset; that's useful information about how overwhelming the feeling is, not a wrong answer. Revisit the map together after a real anger episode to see if a new spot needs adding.

fields.label: Color or mark where you feel anger in your body.
What calming action goes with this spot?
Which spot shows up first when you start to get angry?
Grown-up: which spot did you notice on your child today?
What would you add to the map after today?

title: Brave Body Comic Strip
summary: A child draws a comic of a scary body moment and the steps that helped.
goal: Use it to turn a hard moment into a story the child can retell calmly.
body_md: Have the child draw a three or four panel comic covering what their body started doing, what they thought was happening, what helped, and how it ended; the parent's job is to sit alongside and ask about each panel without correcting the child's version, and if the child wants to skip the scary panel, let them draw it small instead of leaving it out.

fields.label: Panel one: what did my body start doing?
Panel two: what did I think was happening?
Panel three: what did I do, or what did a grown-up do to help?
Panel four: how did it end?
What would I tell my body next time?

title: Sorry and Solution Cards Craft
summary: A child decorates cards used to repair after a conflict at home.
goal: Use it to give a child a concrete script for repairing after a blowup.
body_md: Have the child decorate a small set of cards, each holding a simple repair phrase or gesture like a hug or starting over, and keep them in a shared spot in the house; the parent's role is to model picking a card after their own misstep too, not only hand them to the child, and watch for the ritual being used to end a conversation before feelings are actually heard.

fields.label: What could I say when I want to make things better after a fight?
Draw or write one thing that helps me calm down first.
Who in my family will I practice this with?
What does it feel like after we use a card?

title: Growing Skills Tree Craft
summary: A child builds a tree that fills in with leaves for things they've gotten better at.
goal: Use it to give a child visible evidence of growth, not only fixed praise.
body_md: Have the child draw or build a bare tree, then add a leaf whenever they notice something they can now do better than before, like tying shoes or being brave at a checkup; the parent's role is to prompt for the before version each time so the growth is visible, not just praise the current skill, and watch for a child wanting to add leaves for things not yet actually practiced.

fields.label: Draw your tree with no leaves yet.
What is one thing you can do now that used to be hard?
Add a leaf and write or draw that thing on it.
What do you want to add a leaf for next?

title: Friendship Starter Cue Cards Craft
summary: A child decorates cards with lines for starting or joining a conversation.
goal: Use it to give a child something concrete to say instead of freezing up.
body_md: Have the child decorate a small stack of cards, each with a simple opener like can I play too or what's your favorite game, then practice saying each one out loud with the parent before trying it at school or a playdate; the parent's role is to role-play both parts and celebrate any attempt at using a card, not only the ones that land well.

fields.label: Write or draw one thing I could say to start talking to someone.
Practice saying it out loud to a grown-up first.
Who could I try this with this week?
What happened when I tried it?

title: Missing You Meter Craft
summary: A child builds and colors a dial that shows how much they miss someone each day.
goal: Use it to give a child language for changing grief intensity instead of one flat feeling.
body_md: Have the child decorate a paper dial with a moving arrow or paperclip spinner, labeling sections from 'a little' to 'a lot,' then set it where the parent can see it. Each evening the parent asks the child to move the arrow and briefly says what they notice, without pushing for more detail than the child offers. Children often move the arrow quickly and go back to playing, which is normal grief for their age; the parent's job is steady noticing, not a long conversation every time. Flag it as a caution if the arrow stays stuck on 'a lot' for many days in a row.

fields.label: I am making a meter to show how much I miss someone.
Today my meter says I miss them…
One thing that made today's number go up or down…
One thing that helps me when the number is high…
Something I want to tell the person I miss…

title: Okay Not Okay Touch Sort Craft
summary: A child sorts picture cards into okay and not okay touch, then decorates a keep card.
goal: Use it to build a child's vocabulary for touch safety rules in an age-appropriate way.
body_md: Give the child simple picture cards (a high-five, a hug from a stranger, a doctor visit with a parent present) to sort into 'okay' and 'not okay' piles, then have them decorate a small card listing their own safe adults to keep. This stays at the level of general safety rules, never asking the child to describe their own experiences. If a child discloses any abuse during the activity, stop, respond calmly, and follow your mandated reporting duties right away rather than continuing the craft. The parent reviews the finished safe-adults card together at home.

fields.label: I am sorting cards into okay touch and not okay touch.
One okay touch is…
One not okay touch is…
A safe grown-up I can tell if something feels not okay is…
What I can say if a touch feels not okay…

title: Coping Spinner Wheel Craft
summary: A child builds a spinner of coping ideas to use when big feelings show up.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful, physical way to pick a coping skill in the moment.
body_md: Help the child decorate a paper wheel divided into sections, each drawn with one coping idea the child chose themselves (squeeze a pillow, get a hug, draw, jump in place), attach a spinning arrow with a paper fastener, and post it somewhere accessible. When a big feeling hits, the parent invites the child to spin instead of picking for them, which keeps the choice in the child's hands and lowers a power struggle over which skill to use. Some children spin repeatedly hoping for a favorite section; that's fine early on, and the parent can gently note it rather than restrict spins.

fields.label: I am building a spinner of things that help me feel better.
One thing I'll put on my spinner is…
Today I spun and landed on…
Did it help? A little, some, or a lot…
One more idea I want to add to my spinner…

title: Real vs Edited Pictures Sorting Craft
summary: A child sorts printed pictures into real and edited piles, then builds a poster about it.
goal: Use it to build a child's early media literacy about altered appearance images.
body_md: Print or cut out a mix of ordinary snapshot photos and obviously edited or filtered images, and have the child sort them into 'real' and 'made to look different' piles, then glue their sorted favorites onto a poster with simple labels. Use the sorting to talk about how pictures people see online are often changed, without naming specific bodies as good or bad in the process. Parents can extend this at home by pointing out an edited photo together when one comes up naturally, keeping the tone curious rather than alarmed.

fields.label: I am sorting pictures into real and made to look different.
One clue that told me a picture was edited…
A real picture I liked and why…
One thing I want to remember when I see pictures online…

title: Mirror Move Communication Game
summary: A pairs game where one player mirrors the other's slow movements without talking.
goal: Use it to warm up a group's nonverbal attention and reading of another person's cues.
body_md: Pairs face each other and one player leads with slow movements while the other mirrors as closely as possible without either speaking, switching leaders halfway through; then the group debriefs on what it took to stay in sync. Pairs often speed up or start laughing and drop the mirroring; that's fine to let happen and then ask what broke the connection. Works well as an opener before a session on communication or attention.

fields.label: Who led first, and who followed?
What made it easy to stay in sync?
What made it hard?
How did it feel to lead versus to follow?
What does this remind you of in a real conversation?

title: Puzzle Box Teamwork Challenge
summary: A timed group challenge to solve a set of small puzzles together using only teamwork.
goal: Use it to surface a group's real problem-solving habits under a bit of time pressure.
body_md: Give the group a handful of small puzzles or riddles to solve together within a set time limit, with a rule that no one person can hold or solve a puzzle alone. Groups often let one confident member take over; if that happens, let it play out and raise it directly in the debrief rather than intervening mid-challenge. The debrief question matters more than whether the group finishes in time.

fields.label: What role did you naturally fall into during the challenge?
Did everyone's ideas get heard? Why or why not?
What worked well as a team?
What would you do differently next time?
How does this compare to how your group usually solves problems?

title: Mindful Freeze Game
summary: A movement game where players freeze on a signal and notice one sense for a full minute.
goal: Use it to give a group a playful, embodied taste of a mindful pause.
body_md: Players move around the room until a bell or clap signals freeze, then hold still for a full minute while silently noticing one assigned sense, sound, touch, or sight, before moving again on the next signal. Younger players often want to talk or peek at others during the freeze; a quiet reminder that noticing is silent usually resets it. Rotate through all the senses over a few rounds before the debrief.

fields.label: Which sense did you notice this round?
What's one thing you noticed that you'd normally miss?
Was it easy or hard to stay still?
Which sense was hardest to focus on?
When could you try a freeze like this on your own?

title: Habit Highway Board Game
summary: A board game where players advance by completing small habit-building actions each turn.
goal: Use it to make practicing a new habit feel like play instead of one more chore.
body_md: Players take turns rolling a die and moving along a simple paper highway, landing on spaces that ask them to name or actually do a small piece of a habit they're building, such as naming one cue or describing one obstacle. Players sometimes rush past a space without really answering it; the parent or clinician running the game can ask a quick follow-up before the next turn. Keep the board and add new spaces as the group's habits change.

fields.label: What habit are you building for this game?
Name one cue that reminds you to do your habit.
Name one thing that gets in the way of your habit.
Describe a time this week your habit went well.
What space on the board was hardest to answer?

title: Change Talk Card Game
summary: A card game where players draw prompts about their own reasons for making a change.
goal: Use it to help a group notice and voice their own reasons for wanting to change.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a card with a prompt about reasons for or against a change they're considering, answering out loud before passing to the next player; the group can respond with a follow-up question but not advice. Players sometimes answer in generalities to avoid saying something personal; a follow-up question from the group usually draws out something more specific. Debrief by asking which card's answer surprised the player who drew it.

fields.label: Draw a card and read the prompt out loud.
What's your honest answer?
What's one reason you might not want to change?
What's one reason you might?
Which of your own answers surprised you?

title: Five Senses Grounding Relay
summary: A turn-based group game where each player names a present-moment sensory detail.
goal: Use it to practice quick grounding as a shared, low-pressure group skill.
body_md: Players sit in a circle and pass a small object; whoever holds it names one thing they can currently see, hear, feel, smell or taste, then passes it on for a new turn. Keep the pace brisk and light, and if someone freezes, let them pass and try again next round rather than putting them on the spot. This works well as a session opener when the group seems keyed up, and the debrief should stay in the present moment rather than opening into any one person's history.

fields.label: One thing you can see right now.
One thing you can hear right now.
One thing you can feel right now.
Debrief: which sense was easiest for you to notice today?
Debrief: how does your body feel now compared to before we started?

title: Worry or Fact Card Sort Game
summary: Players take turns sorting statement cards into worry piles and fact piles.
goal: Use it to build quick, shared practice telling a worry apart from a checked fact.
body_md: Prepare a deck of short statement cards mixing worries with verifiable facts, and have players take turns drawing one and sorting it into a worry pile or a fact pile, explaining their reasoning to the group. Disagreement is the useful part; let the group debate a card rather than settling it too fast. People often sort a worry into the fact pile because it feels certain; use those moments to name the difference between feeling sure and being sure. Close with a debrief on which cards were hardest to sort and why.

fields.label: Read your card out loud to the group.
Worry pile or fact pile: where does it go, and why?
Does anyone see it differently?
Debrief: which card was hardest to sort today?
Debrief: what made a worry feel like a fact in the moment?

title: Behavioral Activation Snakes and Ladders
summary: A board game where ladders are small activated steps and snakes are avoidance.
goal: Use it to make behavioral activation steps visible and a little bit playful.
body_md: Build a simple board with the client or group where landing on a ladder square means naming one small activity that lifted mood before, and landing on a snake square means naming one avoidance pattern that has crept in. Players take turns rolling and moving, and roleplaying the ladder square out loud, even briefly, adds more than just reading it silently. Some players want to skip the snake squares; let the group notice that pull and name it rather than forcing a confession. Debrief on which squares felt most true today.

fields.label: Ladder square: name one small activity that has lifted your mood before.
Snake square: name one avoidance pattern you've noticed lately.
Which square did you land on this turn?
Debrief: which ladder could you actually try this week?
Debrief: which snake would be hardest to climb back up from?

title: Urge Surfing Board Game
summary: Players move a token along a wave-shaped board as an urge rises and falls.
goal: Use it to practice riding out an urge as a shared, turn-based activity.
body_md: Draw or print a simple wave-shaped path and have players take turns rolling a die to move a token along it, narrating what an urge at that point on the wave might feel like and one thing that could help ride it out. Reaching the top of the wave without 'giving in' by moving off the board is the shared goal, not competing to finish first. Players sometimes want to skip past the peak quickly; slow that turn down since it is the most useful part to practice narrating. Close with a debrief on which coping move on the board felt most realistic.

fields.label: Roll and move: where is your token on the wave?
Describe what an urge at this point might feel like.
Name one thing that could help you ride out this point.
Debrief: which point on the wave is hardest for you in real life?
Debrief: which coping move felt most realistic to actually use?

title: Cool Down Card Race Game
summary: Players race to name a calming strategy after drawing a frustrating scenario card.
goal: Use it to build fast, shared recall of calming strategies under mild pressure.
body_md: Prepare a deck of short frustrating scenario cards, such as losing a game or being interrupted, and have players take turns drawing one and racing to name a calming strategy before a short timer runs out. Getting a strategy out under the timer, even an imperfect one, is the point, not being clever; keep the mood light and let players cheer each other on. Some players freeze under the timer; let them ask the group for a hint rather than passing in silence. Debrief on which strategies actually felt doable versus which just sounded good.

fields.label: Read your scenario card out loud.
Name a calming strategy before the timer runs out.
Did you beat the timer? How did it feel?
Debrief: which strategy would you actually use in real life?
Debrief: which one just sounded good but wouldn't work for you?

title: Panic Alarm Board Race
summary: A short board game where landing on a coping space earns a bonus move.
goal: Use it to rehearse panic coping steps in a low-pressure, playful format.
body_md: Draw a simple path board with squares that are either a body sensation or a coping skill; players take turns rolling and moving, naming the sensation or acting out the coping skill to earn an extra space, and the first to finish wins; debrief on which coping space felt most doable, and slow down any player who is racing through the naming step to win faster.

fields.label: Which coping space would you want to land on first?
Which sensation square felt easiest to name?
Which coping skill felt hardest to actually do?
Which one will you try for real this week?

title: Kindness Points Family Challenge
summary: Family members earn points for small kind acts and reflect on them together.
goal: Use it to make everyday cooperation and kindness visible and noticed.
body_md: Each family member, including the parents, logs one small kind act toward another member each day on a shared board, tallies it at the end of the week, and takes turns naming an act that stood out to them; watch for it drifting into sibling competition, and steer the debrief back toward noticing rather than counting who did more.

fields.label: What kind act will I try to do for someone in my family today?
Whose kind act toward me stood out this week?
Which was easier, giving kindness or noticing it?
What is one kind act we want to keep doing after this week?

title: New Parent Bingo
summary: A bingo card of common new-parent moments played in a support group.
goal: Use it to normalize the range of new-parent experience in a light format.
body_md: Each square names a common moment, like crying in the bathroom, forgetting to eat, or googling something worrying at 2am; players mark squares that match their week and call bingo when a row fills, then the group debriefs on which square surprised them to see written down; let anyone skip a square that feels too close to real distress that day.

fields.label: Which square matched your week exactly?
Which square surprised you to see written down?
Which square would you add for next time?
What was it like to hear others share the same square?

title: Social Risk Ladder Dice Game
summary: Rolls a die to attempt increasingly bold social micro-challenges in session.
goal: Use it to rehearse graded social risk-taking in a playful, low-stakes format.
body_md: Rank six small social challenges from easiest to hardest, such as three seconds of eye contact, asking someone's name, or disagreeing politely, and assign one to each number on a die; players take turns rolling and attempting that number's challenge with another player, then the group debriefs on what made it easier or harder than expected; let a player trade down one level rather than skip a hard roll.

fields.label: Which challenge felt easiest when you rolled it?
Which challenge felt hardest?
What made a challenge easier once you actually tried it?
Which challenge would you want to practice again for real?

title: Grief Support Bingo
summary: A bingo card of small support actions that players check off and discuss.
goal: Use it to make asking for and offering grief support feel doable in a group.
body_md: Give each player a bingo card filled with small support actions instead of numbers — things like 'texted someone the person's name,' 'let myself cry for two minutes,' or 'said no to an event I wasn't ready for.' Over the week between sessions, players mark a square each time they do or receive one of the actions, and the group compares cards at the next meeting, going row by row on what helped. A sparse card in a hard week is data about capacity, not a failure to play. Close with a debrief question: which square was hardest to earn, and why?

fields.label: One square I marked this week was…
What made that action possible for me…
One square I couldn't get to and why…

title: Safe Adults Scavenger Hunt Game
summary: Kids take turns finding safe-adult cues around a room, then debrief on their own list.
goal: Use it to help a group of children practice naming safe adults in their own life.
body_md: Hide picture cards showing traits of safe adults (someone who listens, someone the child knows well, someone who keeps promises) around the room, and have children take turns finding one card per round and reading its trait aloud. Afterward, have each child name one real safe adult in their life who fits a trait from the cards. Keep it focused on identifying support, never on any past event; if a child discloses abuse during the debrief, pause the game, respond calmly, and follow your mandated reporting duties before continuing. Debrief question: what makes someone easy to tell things to?

title: Coping Skills Draw and Guess Game
summary: Players sketch a coping skill in turns while others guess it, then debrief what stuck.
goal: Use it to make naming and remembering coping skills fun for a group.
body_md: Give each player a turn drawing a coping skill from a hidden list — no words or letters allowed — while the rest of the group guesses within a set time limit before rotating to the next artist. Keep score loosely or skip it entirely; the value is in seeing the same handful of skills drawn and guessed repeatedly until they stick. Some players freeze up when it's their turn to draw; let them choose from three cards instead of drawing blind if that helps. Close with a debrief question: which skill would you actually reach for this week?

title: Approach or Avoid Card Game
summary: Players draw scenario cards and vote approach or avoid before comparing reasoning.
goal: Use it to practice spotting avoidance patterns together in a low-stakes group format.
body_md: Deal out scenario cards describing a feared situation, not necessarily the players' own fears, and on each turn the group votes approach or avoid before the card-holder reveals what a values-driven choice might look like. Rotate the card-holder each round so everyone gets a turn leading. Some players will vote avoid reflexively for every card; use that as a debrief moment rather than correcting it in the round. Close with the debrief question: which vote surprised you about yourself?
